speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I again have the honour to present a petition in the House of Commons concerning the Government's plan to cut back on VIA services.
The people who have signed this petition express their concern with regard to that issue. I point out in presenting this petition that there were 65 students and 14 chaperones from The Pas, Manitoba, who wished to go to
Churchill and made bookings in February of this year to go at the end of June. They were told recently that there were no cars available to put them on, even though they had made bookings three and a half months ago. It took the intervention of the office of a Member of Parliament for those students to be able to ride on VIA.
The Government claims: "Use it or lose it". Students cannot possibly use it because the Government of Canada will not provide the necessary equipment.

subtopic: PETITIONS

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to present a petition on behalf of a number of people from Kamloops, British Columbia, who are concerned about the Government's intention to eliminate passenger rail service in the country.
The petitioners are drawing to the attention of the Government all the reasons for continuing with passenger rail service. Basically, they are calling upon Parliament now, since the Government refuses to listen, to maintain, to improve and to modernize VIA rail service, particularly in those areas of the country where it can provide a more rapid, economical, safe, convenient and environmentally sound alternative to other means of transportation.

subtopic: PETITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a second petition on a different topic. They are aware of a number of countries that receive arms, military or paramilitary equipment from Canada, countries in which there are obvious abuses of human rights. They are asking the Canadian Government to stop this process of militarizing our economy.

speechtext:
There is an expression, "You are darned if you do and you are darned if you don't." If you rise too quickly you get embarrassed by the Speaker, and then something else if you rise too late.
Borrowing Authority
The point is that I simply want to make a few remarks on behalf of the Minister of State for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs (Mr. McDermid) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) who is responsible for the Bill. I want to indicate their thanks and appreciation to the members of the legislative committee who dealt with the Bill in a prompt manner. I noticed the Bill was introduced on April 27 of this year and we are now seeking third reading not too long after. That is appreciated and indicates Parliament and the House can under the appropriate circumstances proceed with some dispatch to deal with the important matter of government affairs.
The co-operation of the committee will assist the Government in moving ahead with the program of orderly debt management by dealing with the substantial cash requirements of the Government of Canada. I, on behalf of the Minister, thank all the Members of the House who co-operated in the manner in which they did to bring this Bill to its present state in a relatively quick manner.
I want to remind the House of the grave financial position of the Government of Canada as represented by the needs carefully outlined in this Bill. We are in a very difficult situation with the $320 billion debt and a deficit in this fiscal year which will run to $30 billion. It is the task of all Members to participate in the reduction of and the appropriate management of this debt.
Canadians, as Hon. Members know, have to make some choices. We would all like to keep every government program intact without reduction, but that costs money and the money can only come either from increased taxation or from piling up additional debt. We want to avoid additional debt. It has become very costly to absorb that over 35 per cent of every revenue dollar which goes to the debt. Therefore, we have to make these choices, but I am sure it is with some reluctance that the Government deals with the realities of the financial situation by reducing government expenditures with obvious effects.
I may point out, as I have on previous occasions in the House, that given the realities of our fiscal situation, some of the regions of Canada which appear to suffer most from any reductions have something to their credit. The Government of Canada has increased very dramatically over the last year the transfer payments to those

June 12. 1989
Borrowing Authority
regions of the country, particularly Atlantic Canada, that suffer as a result of regional disparity.
There has been over $186 million paid into Atlantic Canada as a result of transfer payments. In the case of Nova Scotia, it amounted to 19 per cent more than was anticipated. In the case of Prince Edward Island, it has a balanced budget. In the case of Nova Scotia, it is able to look forward to balancing the budget in the next fiscal year. That is something that the Government of Canada will only be able to achieve after a four or five year period.
There are some rays of sunshine in the financial picture of Atlantic Canada, and I hope that the Government's competent management of the national economy and finances will aid that situation in the future so that at some time, probably many years distant, we will not have to face statutory issues like borrowing Bills for the vast amounts of money the Government of Canada needs to meet its obligations.
As I have indicated, it is the duty of a Government to make the hard financial choices that lead in some cases to tough cut-backs in expenditures, but I am sure that Canadians understand and appreciate that their choice is very simple. They either pay more taxes or receive something less in Government services.
As I talk to my constituents, I find that they do not want to pay any more taxes. They do not want to contribute any more to the revenues of the Government of Canada. They are at the tax limit, so the only hope and prospect for the future of all Canadians is to have better management of the financial situation and the national economy, and that is what the Government is doing, through this very Bill which is now before the House for third reading.
So that Hon. Members will understand that there is hope for the future, particularly for Atlantic Canada, I want to mention the free trade initiative which we think will bring great benefits to Atlantic Canada. Hon. Members do not have to take my word for it. The Premier of New Brunswick who received a unanimous endorsement from the electorate of that province said in a recent speech made in the City of Halifax that Atlantic Canada is now part of the over-all economic picture. Atlantic Canadians now have opportunities that they did not have before. The challenge in Atlantic Canada is to take advantage of those opportunities, as Premier McKenna said. I hope Members of the Liberal Party will pay attention to the words he spoke in the city of Halifax
before a group of business people. We have the opportunities and the potential and we have to go ahead and meet that challenge and get the job done. We will improve the economy of Canada through the free enterprise system and through individual entrepreneurship and enterprise. That is how we will get the funds to pay for the services and reduce the need for borrowing.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first I want to applaud your discretion and judgment in allowing the Hon. Member to speak first. After his presentation, my job becomes so much easier. He has opened up so many interesting lines of inquiry and examination that we could be here all morning simply discussing the first topic alone, the question of the management of the economy.
The Hon. Member sat down two minutes ago. Now he wants to talk again. It is fascinating how slow his reaction time is. He only thinks of what he wants to say after he sits down.
Through this borrowing authority Bill, we have the opportunity to look at the stewardship of the Government, its management of the economy, its so-called economic blueprint, and we have an opportunity to determine whether the heavy requirement the borrowing authority puts on the capital markets of Canada is justified, if it will be an effective, useful and fair rendering of economic policy and management for Canada as we enter into some tumultuous and turbulent times.
This Government has been a bit lucky, both bad and good, because much of the debate in this House has been concentrated on the fiasco of the release of the phantom Budget by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the attempts of the Government to cover it up. Much of the attention has been deflected from the real Budget, the Budget that will have a long-term impact on Canada, the Budget which will fundamentally restructure and reorganize the economic fabric of Canada and our attempts to ensure that there is something called a fair political economy in Canada.
If I may, I would like to begin by challenging the Hon. Member who just spoke on behalf of the Government to prove some of his assertions about so-called effective economic management. I think the first criteria for effective economic management by the Government is honesty, telling the truth, putting the facts before the people. If the Government has any responsibility, it is to ensure that Canadians fully understand the economic
June 12, 1989

conditions they face and the options and choices before them.
Less than six or seven months ago during the election campaign, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) said that the Government would never touch unemployment insurance, that it is sacred for forever. There was a man of honesty and probity, a man we could trust implicitly. Now, however, we have before us a total and complete chopping apart of the unemployment insurance program.
I read all the newspapers. I am told that the Minister of Finance is a paragon of virtue, that he is the most honest Minister in the Cabinet. They say that he is the one in which the credibility of the Government resides. What happened during the election campaign? He was calling everyone else liars and saying that he had the money in the bank, he was prepared to pay for these programs. He said that these were not promises but commitments because the money was already in the till and everything was going fine. Then in his Budget, he slashed every single one of those commitments.
Day care for children is perhaps one of the most important programs for providing a sense of justice and fairness and for allowing women to have a fair share of the job market. The Minister cut that program. Perhaps I missed something. I was so busy campaigning during the election campaign, perhaps I missed the Minister of Finance telling us that he would cancel the day care program.
I recall hearing the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance saying on television that they were firmly committed to day care. Now, all of a sudden, a few short months later, have conditions ever changed. All of a sudden there has been a revelation. On the road to Damascus, the Minister of Finance had a new revelation. He found that he can no longer pay for day care.
Did Hon. Members hear the Minister of Finance, that paragon of integrity, talking during the election campaign about cutting back on VIA Rail, a program that is essential for many of the regions, including the Atlantic Region, about which the Hon. Member just spoke? We just received the secret report. About 89 per cent of the
Borrowing Authority
lines will be cut in the Atlantic region and 70 per cent of the lines will be cut in western Canada. For the life of me, I cannot recall hearing the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) saying that six months ago. Is it not amazing what has been discovered in six months? It seems to me that on the level of honesty, fairness and judgment, we could expect the Government to at least be consistent.
The question I asked at the beginning of the debate was: Up until November 21, did the Government know what the economy looked like, the drastic and Draconian difficulties that we faced, and simply was not telling Canadians? In other words it covered up, or was it so stupid and totally blinded that the Government and its officials did not know? Either one, when measuring it against the judgment of a Government, does not look too good.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: They are dumb and stupid.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Maybe it was a combination. Maybe the Government did not know, did not care, and did not make the effort to find out.
Certainly there has been nothing that we have seen since this session opened in terms of all the announcements on unemployment insurance, day care, and regional programs from which we got the slightest suspicion or inkling back at the time the Government was asking the Canadian people for an accounting. That is the way the parliamentary system should work. A Government stands or falls on its record. If its record was so good, why was it not honest about it? Why was it not fair about it?
Unfortunately that was not only a problem during the election. It is a problem now. That same sense of camouflage, that same masquerade, is perpetrated on a continuous basis. It is fascinating to look at the Budget which stated that Canadians were going to have to sacrifice. We have a deficit in front of us. Members of the House recognize that it is one of the questions that has to be examined carefully and is part of the economic framework of this country. However, surely Canadians have a right to expect their Government to be honest

June 12, 1989
Borrowing Authority
with them about who is going to bear the burden and how fair the apportionment of that sacrifice will be.
In the Budget Papers there was no attempt to describe in any real way who is going to pay for the Government's mistakes. Who is going to pay for the escalating deficits that have multiplied over the last four years? The deficit has doubled in the last four or five years of this Government. We conducted our own study to find out. We got the StatsCan model developed by the Government and ran the figures in the Budget through to see who would be affected.
Those who are going to carry the biggest burden and who will make the toughest sacrifices are families with children. Is that not a real judgment on behalf of the Conservative Party of Canada? The people who are going to carry the heaviest burden, pay the heaviest tax load, and lose the most income as a result of this specific Budget are working families with two kids. They will have $582 less income under this Budget than they would have had last year. That does not include the four years previous. A family with two children and an income of around $30,000 to $40,000 will have $582 less. That means that eight out of every ten taxpayers will lose a substantial amount under this Budget.
The Minister of Finance stated that this was a Budget that would take from the rich and give to the poor. Somehow I do not understand why a working family with two children and making $35,000 a year is called rich by the Conservative Government. They are the ones who are carrying the burden of this Government's so-called economic blueprint.
The Minister of Finance also stated that the Government is being particularly charitable to senior citizens. The only people from whom we are clawing back and scratching out the living are those who are very rich, the top 4 per cent. I would be glad to send this study to members of the Tory back-benches opposite. They might want to read some honesty for a change. The real impact is that more than half of the senior citizens, over 2.1 million, will be receiving less income under this Budget than previously. It is not 4 per cent. It is 50 per cent. That is a far cry from the declarations of the Minister of Finance in the House day after day. That is a big gap between reality and what the Minister says is the truth. Now, added to families with children are senior citizens who will be paying a substantially heavier burden.
Fet us look at the poor. The Government has stated that this is being done in order that extra income can be targeted to give to those most in need. Day after day we have listened to the Minister of Finance saying that he really is Florence Nightingale with the lamp. He is going to go out there and give to the poor. Instead, the same study shows that over 800,000 families earning $15,000 or lower will have less income as a result of this Budget. Can that be considered to be targeting help for the poor? We are targeting them all right. We are putting an arrow right between their eyes. We are targeting their limited income.
This is happening at a time when, according to the Canadian Council on Social Development, there are more than one-quarter of a million homeless in the country. We are talking about taking money from those people who cannot even afford to find a house. That is considered to be the "lady bountiful" approach of this Government. It is incredible to think of the dishonesty and duplicity that is being given to Canadians in the ad campaigns that are being paid for by the taxpayers. They are not being told the truth.
This Budget zeros in on families with kids, senior citizens, and the poor, yet it does nothing at all on the other side. I read nothing in the Budget whatsoever that would give any reassurance that the quarter of a million families who are homeless would receive any form of assistance.
There is an important trend taking place that should set off an alarm bell in every single Member and should be recognized as one of the great tragedies occurring in our so-called modern society. Fifty per cent of those who are now considered poor in this country are younger people, particularly single parents with children. Fifty per cent of those living below the poverty line are younger families. They are no longer only senior citizens. We are now adding substantially to the pool of poor people, especially those with children.
The new Minister of State for Housing must be embarrassed and ashamed. When he was a member of the government side, from time to time he had the courage to rise and ask his cabinet colleagues: "What are you going to do about the homeless? What are you going to do about housing?" Now he has been appointed to that job where one would have thought because of his previous record in the House he would have tackled it with zeal and diligence, he finds that his budget has been cut back. He has less money to deal with the problem
June 12, 1989

than there was before. He knows that his Minister of Finance is taking money out of people's pockets that could otherwise go to pay for housing projects.
What Government with a sense of fairness would allow that type of discrimination to take place? What values are we telling Canadians that the Government represents when it is prepared to take money from families and money from poor people, yet not provide that money for any more targeting, direction, or services?
The Hon. Member who opened this debate stated that Canadians knew what a difficult time it was. Yes, it is a difficult time, because the Government makes it difficult on so many Canadians. It is creating the difficulties because it is not being fair and honest about the economic conditions being faced by Canadians.
That same gap and discrimination, the fact that the Government is creating a two level society, a society of two Canadas, is becoming more apparent in the regions of Canada, the hinterlands of Canada, and the places where people have less power and growth.
For years those regions have relied on fishing, lumbering, mining, or the basic resources of this country which have been the creators of wealth for more than 120 years. Because one lives in northern Manitoba, in the fishing outports of the Atlantic, or in the sawmills towns of British Columbia, one has to provide for periods of very intense work and then an income support for the other portion of the year.
One of the things I recognized when I was Minister of Employment was that the unemployment insurance program was the essential that allowed our resource based industries and our resource based regions to maintain an effective workforce; to keep people in those regions so they could continue to fish, farm, mine and lumber; and to provide those kinds of resources which are still a source of wealth, with some sense of dignity and with some sense of honour.
They are hard working people, but they can only fish for 14 weeks a year in certain parts of the Atlantic and West Coast. They can only mine during certain parts of
Borrowing Authority
the year. They can only lumber during certain parts of the year. Therefore, there has to be a balance.
One of the ways we did that in the unemployment insurance program was through a particular commitment of the Government of Canada to guarantee an income base through its own investment on behalf of the rest of us. I considered that a program of real honour, as well as smart economics.
One thing this Government lacks is the commitment to the people of Canada. There is no commitment to the citizens who work in the resource regions across Canada to maintain their families and to keep them there. The real basic underlying philosophy of this Government is that that does not count any more.
The Government is prepared to give incentives to big corporations to put in more machinery, to give these corporations capital write-offs and depletion allowances so they can bring in more machinery and more technology, but they can put the workers on the scrap heap.
As a result, what the Government will do is build up the big cities, increase the housing inflation rates in Toronto by 30 per cent or 40 per cent, have overcrowded roads in the golden horseshoe, create a Canada of three or four large cities, and the rest of Canada will not count. It is a strange, perverted, distorted view of this country. It does not fit with the history, tradition, or even the good economics of this country.
The Government does not stop with gutting the public commitment to the unemployment insurance program. It goes on. It does not stop there. What is the next announcement of that the enlightened Minister of Transport who has had such a string of successes as the Pearson Airport, the Gander air crash, and now the cut-backs in VIA Rail? What did the Minister of Transport do? He has had a singular record of disasters unknown in the history of this country. Now the Minister stands up and says: "I had no responsibility for VIA Rail".
The Minister has never bothered to examine, in the slightest way, what the economic impact will be in cancelling the line between Melville and Saskatoon, the line between Winnipeg and Thompson, or the line on the east shore of Nova Scotia. There is no analysis. There is no impact study to ask: "Do people need that form of transportation? What does it do in terms of making sure

June 12. 1989
Borrowing Authority
there is no monopoly? Are they restricted simply to one bus line, which can then charge a going rate?
There has been no attempt to give us in Parliament or anywhere else an explanation for that severe cut-back, no attempt to hold public hearings, no attempt to talk to the premiers or the local municipal councillors to work out a plan. It is going to be an arbitrary initiative, completely and totally unrelated to the economic reality of those regions.
If that were not enough, it goes on by cutting back the bases, the military budget. Let us accept, for sake of argument, that some cuts have to take place and that Departments have to effect them. Surely one would expect that those judgments that are being made by the Government would be based upon some effective or useful analysis, some judgment based upon reality, some decision based upon whether the bases are good or bad.
I will give an example. I was in Portage la Prairie on Friday. I met with the residents of the area, the Chamber of Commerce, and the municipal councillors. I looked at what was happening in that area. The military people on the base itself have yet to receive any instructions, any orders, or any analysis as to why that base will be closed. The community has yet to receive a visit from the Minister of National Defence or any other Minister. The Member of Parliament has not been seen in that area for six or eight weeks.
They ask the question: "What are you going to do with training?" At the Portage la Prairie base, there are three different forms of training. There is training for instructors, helicopters, and preliminary training. The Government sort of spread it around that it was to privatize the primary training. There was no discussion about what it would do with helicopter training or the training for instructors.
What is the alternative? There are only three other places on the Prairies to go to. The base in Winnipeg is already overcrowded and the air space is cluttered. The Moose Jaw and Edmonton bases have the same problem. Where is the training function of the Department of Defence going to go? No one has the foggiest notion. Obviously the Minister does not know. The defence
officials do not know, because they were never asked by the Government to do that kind of analysis or judgment.
The decision was made again in an arbitrary way without any consultation, feeling, empathy, or sympathy for that community which is losing a $50-million investment and 700 or 800 workers. An enormous hole will be torn into its economy, and they cannot even get anyone to talk to them or explain to them what is going on.
That is being repeated right across this country. It is happening in Summerside and everywhere we go. It is simply stonewall. That is the order of the day. The Government keeps a closed mind and closed heart to those kinds of decisions which are being made.
My colleague from York West offered an alternative in a very generous way. He said: "We have a base called Downsview in Toronto. We would much rather turn it into housing for all those people who cannot get housing. Let the functions of that base go to Summerside or Portage la Prairie". The Government does not even listen to him. It just rejects it out of hand and does not even look at the alternative.
I suggested to the Minister of Defence in a letter to begin negotiating with NATO allies to see if they want to do similar kinds of training on these bases. I received a letter back from the Minister of Defence stating: "Sorry, I am not interested". The Minister does not have the least concern about finding an alternative for the people of Portage la Prairie, Summerside, or anywhere else.
I ask why. A Government has some sense of responsibility. The reason the system works is that we are not the same as the private sector. The reason we go through all the rigmarole of having an election and putting people in their seats in Parliament is because the public sector should have a different way of doing things. It should be responsible, accountable, and sensitive to individual needs. The people of Portage la Prairie do not sit in the boardrooms of big corporations. That is why they elect a Member of Parliament. It is so they can have access and feel they have an opportunity to participate in making decisions that are going to affect them in a direct way. I am sure that will be taken care of in the next election. Make no mistake about that.

speechtext:
Famous last words. There are five Liberal Members of Parliament from the Province of Manitoba from the last election. There will be ten the next time.
By the way, Madam Speaker, for the Member who just spoke, I will not bother sending him a Christmas card for the next Christmas party because he will not be here.
The fact of the matter is that it reflects that this is a Government that has lost its sense of governing, its sense that there is a public responsibility, a sense of public service. When Conservatives make tough economic decisions-and no one says that they should not make them-they should do it with sensitivity and nobility to ensure that the interests of the most defenceless, the least advantaged, are not hurt. What we see time after time in the Budget is that this is simply not the case.
I could continue with examples of the way in which this Government, through its economic decisions, is fostering division and separation of Canada into different classes. It is creating a hierarchy of Canadians-those most privileged with the most access who do not have to pay their share of taxes, and those least favoured, least privileged, who are most separated and most distanced from the centres of power. That is a recipe of disaster because we know from our history that the only way we can hold ourselves together and knit a fabric is by some real attempt by the Government of Canada, a strong national Government with some sense of will, to bring it together.
I want to speak about the question of economic management, which is equally critical. The Government must show some sense of competence and effective management. Again, during the election we were told that the signing of the Free Trade Agreement would open the portals of paradise for Canadians. We were told that we would be ushered into the land of milk and honey, that the moment it was signed unemployment would drop and a vast market would open up, that all the problems with the Americans would be resolved, and that we would live in a land of salvation forever.
According to the Jimmy Swaggart of Canadian politics, otherwise known as the Prime Minister of Canada, we were guaranteed eternal salvation for our souls. Let us
Borrowing Authority
see what has happened in the last six months. Interest rates have gone up three points. The dollar has risen by 15 points. Our export market with the Americans is down by 15 per cent, and our imports have risen by 7 per cent. Our current accounts trade balance is the worst it has been in the last 10 years. Those are the hard statistics from the last six months as a result of the Free Trade Agreement that would open up so-called markets. If they are opening so fast, why are the Americans getting them? Why is it a one way revolving door that they come in and we get pushed out?
After the first six months of operation of the Free Trade Agreement, the softwood lumber industry is in dire straits. I see some of the wise sages on the other side shaking their heads. In fact, I can hear them. The fact is that the Minister for International Trade, who was never known for his broad range of views, admitted in the House of Commons that the softwood lumber industry, the largest employer in Canada, is in dire straits because of the Free Trade Agreement.
As a result of the agreement signed by the former Minister for International Trade, the so-called Hawaiian beach pact for softwood lumber, we are now faced with the situation of 2,000 lay-offs in northern Ontario. Sawmills are closing down virtually every day. Export markets are being lost and a major industry in this country is in real trouble. The problem is that the Government signed an agreement and entrenched it in the Free Trade Agreement. Now it cannot get out of that agreement.
Let us look at another regional problem. Just this morning, about an hour ago, I met with unions and workers from the west coast fish processing plants. Again, the difficulty is that the solutions that should have been available to them once the GATT ruling was made is denied them under the Free Trade Agreement. An export tax to protect the right of Canadian workers on the West Coast to process their own product, a recourse perfectly acceptable under GATT, is denied them under the Free Trade Agreement.
Suddenly 2,000 to 3,000 workers are being faced with the harsh reality of losing their jobs because of what the Government wrote into the Free Trade Agreement, thereby surrendering one of the sovereign rights of any country to apply a tax on any export in order to ensure

June 12. 1989
Borrowing Authority
that value added or processing would take place in that country.

speechtext:
Of course, that goes without saying. I expect that promise of paradise made six months ago must ring awfully hollow to those workers in the fish processing plants who are faced with that harsh reality.
One can do an industry by industry study across the country to see where job losses are occurring. Let us consider the printing industry, for instance. There is a small family owned printing operation in Winnipeg which printed the telephone books for 50 years. It is a business which employed 60 workers. It was wiped out because under the Free Trade Agreement a huge billion dollar business in Chicago simply underpriced them and put them out of commission.
The Government's own studies show how in industry after industry, business after business, there are major fundamental structural problems occurring because of the Free Trade Agreement. I am holding a number of studies which I brought with me to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade in order to ask the officials and the Minister how they would deal with these problems. These studies, conducted by the Minister's own Department and the Government, included sound recording, paper products, power generation equipment, paints and coatings, vegetable processing. I asked the officials if they would do something about these problems, and when they would take action.
According to the Budget, there is a dismantling of the programs. As a result of this Free Trade Agreement the Government of Canada has a responsibility to ensure that our industries and businesses can meet those new conditions under which they will have to operate. It will have to ensure that the workers can retrain, that new capital investment can be provided, and that businesses can be defended against harsh and unnecessary attacks. Yet the Government has sat on its hands and refused to take any initiative whatsoever.
The Minister for International Trade has stalled in his tracks. We never see him here because he is visiting the world capitals and bringing the message about how other countries should not sign bilateral trade agreements. I was quite intrigued to read the communique signed by
the Minister for International Trade at the OECD, which warned against bilateral trade. The communique stated: "Ministers firmly reject the tendency toward unilateralism and bilateralism, sectoralism and managed trade".
It is fascinating that our Minister for International Trade, the great apostle of the FTA, is now warning Europeans about the dangers of it. Perhaps the Minister has found his own conversion and that is why the Prime Minister will not let him back in the country or the House of Commons. Perhaps the Minister recognizes what a total flop the Free Trade Agreement is, and the Prime Minister will not let him back to tell Canadians about it. He signed the communique and will tell Europeans about it, but he has not yet told Canadians that he thinks bilateralism represents a major threat to world trade.
I agree with the Minister, but we were saying that two years ago. Perhaps he is a late bloomer, or perhaps he finally read the Free Trade Agreement and discovered that it was a mistake. We know that the Government made a mistake, and we are seeing evidence of it every day in Canada.
One of the so-called benefits is to be able to resolve disputes and obtain guaranteed markets. However, there is a major case against the pork producers of Canada, in which the preliminary judgment based upon U.S. trade law is that they will have to pay a new tariff on processed pork products. While that comes as a great surprise, it is even more surprising to realize that rather than give them a resolution to the problem, the Free Trade Agreement created it because according to the FTA we must apply U.S. trade law.
Canadians who read about the hearings before the National Energy Board must be interested in discovering that Canada will guarantee 60 per cent of our natural gas supply to markets south of the border in perpetuity, while our own security of supply and ability to ensure security for Canadian consumers are not equally protected.

speechtext:
George Bush said that he wanted a kinder and compassionate country, but we did not think he meant he would buy Canada to get it.
June 12, 1989

I want to go to one further reference which I think is perhaps the most serious. It appeared in La Presse. It was a study done by a private consulting firm, Venture Economics. It points out that in the first quarter of this year, the number of take-overs and acquisitions equals virtually all the take-overs and acquisitions of the year before. As the study points out, we now have the greatest, largest, single movement of take-overs and acquisitions in the history of this country in the first three months of 1989. What we are facing is the total and complete elimination of Canadian ownership of its subsidiaries. General Electric and Westinghouse are buying back their subsidiaries. That means that our ability to control our own economy and to make decisions in relation to the way we want to operate as Canadians are being closed off. That is part of the agenda as well.
When we look at figure after figure, and argument after argument, we come up with one very clear lesson. One of the hidden agendas in this Budget and one of the cover-ups which is taking place is that this is the next instalment in the Free Trade Agreement. This is the pay-off for the Americans that they did not get in the first round. We have paid them off in the second round in this Budget. All the attacks and eliminations of unemployment insurance, regional development budgets, transportation and agricultural programs are all designed to meet American complaints and concerns before we even get to the negotiating table.
There is this great hoax that there is going to be seven years of negotiation on subsidies. There will not be seven years, we are giving it all away in the first six months of 1989. What have we got left to negotiate, when the Government has already eviscerated and cut off the question of subsidies to unemployment insurance and transportation programs for agriculture? There is nothing left.
We begin to see once again the willingness of the Government, rather than playing it straight and telling Canadians what they really are facing in terms of an economic blueprint, have painted it over and have cosmetics on it. Instead of being forthright, it goes off and takes some more taxpayers' dollars and pays for an advertising program to tell them how great it really is.
Borrowing Authority
It is not that much different from the kind of manipulation and distortion we see going on on the television screens of China this week where they announce that: "No one was really killed." While it is not severe in terms of the taking of human life, it shows the power of government to manipulate and distort, to create the kind of big lie about what is really going on through the power of its own purse and the power of the media. That is why it is so essential that we somehow try to break through that screen and dissipate the fog, to get down to things that are really of crucial concern.
I want to just touch on one other area which I believe has not received the kind of attention it should have in this House because of all the other things that have been breaking around us. That is the way in which this Budget is savaging those least able to help themselves, the most defenceless of people. We have to talk about the way in which this Government is approaching the serious tragedies occurring in the world around us.
Whether it is in the area of international trade or international aid, the Government is showing a callousness which I think is unreported since the Second World War. It takes us back to the 1930s when governments closed its doors to other countries and thought that it could exist in isolation. It thought it could somehow make itself immune from the rigours and the turbulences of the world around it. That is the kind of philosophy being adopted by this Government.
We look at the savage cut-backs to the CIDA program, of hundreds of millions of dollars. I do not care how much the Minister and the Government tries to dance around the issue, there has been a severe undermining of the basic commitment to international aid. This happens at a time when the situation in Third World countries is getting worse and not better. There are more children dying of malnutrition. There are more schools being closed down.
The wages of workers in Third World countries are falling. When the ability of those countries to invest in roads and basic industry is being reduced, this is a government which cuts back in its aid. The reason is because we are absolutely complicit. We are part of the international conspiracy to force many of those countries to pay back debts to private bankers and to use public money coming out of our treasury to the international bank to recycle back to private vaults. As a consequence,

June 12, 1989
Borrowing Authority
we put the most severe extortion on the lives of the people.
If there is any one sort of embarrassment it is that we are so silent about the subject. The Minister of Finance goes off to the meetings of the OECD, or the G-7, all those great international bodies, and whether it is the Brady plan or the Baker plan, they are all designed basically to prop up the private banks of North America and Europe. At the same time, the countries of the Third World are having to totally distort their economies and ruin their environments simply to pay back those bills. We are aiding and abetting in that cause. We then compound the problem by cutting back on aid at the same time.
The North-South Institute, which I think is one of the most respected organizations in this country, and who no one would accuse of being partisan or having a political axe to grind other than the truth, what does it say about this? It says it represents probably the single most important issue to be faced by this Government. It says it both for reasons of what has to take place in the international economy, and also our own economy.
By allowing that kind of failure of the international economic system to continue, Canadians themselves have lost close to $27 billion worth of exports and a 130,000 jobs, simply because we have such a limited perspective and closed point of view. We do not understand that what is really going on in El Salvador, Brazil, or sub-Saharan Africa affects us as much as what happens on the plains of Saskatchewan or in the fishing outports of Newfoundland. We have the same kind of results and the same kind of sense of integration. When we talk about globalization, we are just not talking about big corporations running the world. We are talking about the intrinsic linkage which we have with the seven or eight billion people on this earth, two-thirds of whom are now suffering more this year than they did last year, and more last year than the year before.
One would have thought that under those circumstances and in that kind of condition, that when the Government is presenting an economic blueprint, and trying to foresee the future and look ahead a little bit, it might say: "Look, here is a fundamental responsibility of the people of Canada and through their government we
intend to act." Instead, it crashes the Minister of External Aid at the knees, draws down the Budget and goes along with a plan which is designed internationally to extort money from Third World countries, where we take more in than what we give out. We are all guilty by ourselves. We will pay a price in our environment, our economy and simply as our morality as human beings.
That is why the real failure of this Budget simply goes beyond questions of what happens in the fiscal rates next year or next month.
One would have expected in a new mandate the Government would have made some effort to look at the real economic questions. The real economic questions in Canada are not the deficit reduction. That is only a small part of the problem. The real question is the economy of this country, and this country, as part of a much larger system, is undergoing a fundamental restructuring. It is going to require the best intelligence, competence, honesty and openness to bring Canadians to an understanding of what is going on, and by letting them become part of the examination of the problem and part of the solution instead of putting up walls, closing down information, and hiding behind smokescreens. The only way we can approach these very severe economic problems is through a sharing.
Yet we divide the country. There are labour unions which feel that they are totally isolated from any sense of participation in the management of the country. There are people arriving on VIA Rail trains who say that they do not belong to the economy of the country. They feel as if they cannot talk to anyone in the Government. There are Ministers walking out of meetings, refusing to attend others, and not holding public consultations. They try to bluster their way through. They try to crash their way through in the hope that the people will be bought and sold through this propaganda campaign we see on our TV screens every night. It is a campaign which states: "You have never had it so good. The deficit is a problem, and we are looking after it". That just will not fly.
Canadians are smarter than that. They understand. They learned from the last election when we fought out the trade issue. They have an appetite for an understanding that they have a real role to play in important
June 12, 1989

economic decisions. They cannot be bought off by glitz and glamour and heavy public relations or ad campaigns.

That is not why they voted for you. The fact of the matter is that in the last election they were bought off.
The tactic of the Government is to try valiantly to cover up that type of opportunity and to use modern techniques of propaganda, manipulation and communication distortion to get around it. It succeeds once in a while. It gets by. A negative campaign can be run. One can go around calling others liars. Elowever, the fact is that it is coming home to roost.
We have seen in the House of Commons the Minister of Finance no longer has a shred of credibility left. No one will ever believe again that Minister of Finance. There is no longer any trust or confidence in this Minister of Finance. The only people who do have that are those who lock themselves in to the Tory caucus room on Wednesday mornings and who, through a succession of psychological cheer-leading, get themselves to believe somehow, that the world around them is all right.

The fact is that that is the requirement that we on this side of the House believe has to take place. We really believe at this point in time in looking at the economy of Canada that there is a great deal more to be done than just zeroing in on deficit reduction as is done on the business pages or the Tory caucus room. There are fundamental questions on how to have full employment shared equally across the country in all regions so that people do not feel separated, divorced or that they are being relegated to a hinterland without any sense of concern. Canadians will
Borrowing Authority
still be able to have the right to choose jobs in their own region and not have to retreat or migrate to large urban areas simply to support their families.
We believe very fundamentally that we have a major responsibility to deal with a new reality of international trade and international competition. That will create for Canadians perhaps our biggest test economically. How can we get our research, development and training into some type of effective investment across the country so that we can meet those types of needs without cutting back or reducing those programs?
We believe that in terms of the environment there will have to be some serious judgments made about whether we simply promote unqualified economic growth without seeing that all that growth has very severe environmental costs. It will take some economic reform in the way we make things and do things in order to make sure that those costs will not be passed on to other generations. Those are the economic issues of our time. They are the type of things that we have to examine. We received nothing of the sort in the Budget. We have received nothing of the sort in the economic statements by Ministers. We have seen nothing of the sort in the approach taken by the Minister of Finance.
The Government is asking for approval of a borrowing authority. It needs money. What the country really needs is good, serious economic policy. It needs good management and honesty. It needs some sense of fairness.
We open a session of Parliament with certain prayers. It is probably worth it to close my remarks with a note sent to me by a constituent who puts the calamity and tragedy into its proper religious mode. It states:
Mike Wilson is my shepherd. I am in want. He maketh me to lie down on park benches. He leadeth me beside the still factories. He disturbeth my soul. Yea though I walk through the valley of the shadow of recession, f anticipate no recovery, for he is still with me. He anointeth my small income with great taxes. My expenses runneth over.
Surely unemployment and poverty will follow me all the days of my life. And 1 shall dwell in a mortgaged house forever.
That sums up properly the economic management style of the present Minister of Finance. What it does not set out is the enormous vacuum that exists in all the other areas of crucial economic policy. What the country is crying out for, something which it has an enormous appetite for, is some real choice, some real sense of the judgment that will have to be applied by Canadians in terms of getting our economy right, making it fair.

June 12. 1989
Borrowing Authority
honest and equally shared. That is what the Liberal Party will provide.

speechtext: Elear, hear!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the remarks of my colleague who has just spoken. I must say that when I was here first today to listen to the opening remarks on the third reading stage of Bill C-ll, an Act to provide borrowing authority for billions of dollars not exceeding $24.8 billion, I assumed that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) would be here to begin the debate. Obviously he was not here. I understand why he is not. I do not think that he has any credibility left. We hear and read in every financial newspaper of the country that he should resign, consider resigning or that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should ask for his resignation. It is not surprising that the Minister of Finance would choose not to introduce a borrowing authority calling for Parliament to support the borrowing of $24 billion.
However, one would then assume that a senior Minister, or any Minister, would introduce and explain what the Government plans to do with this $24 billion, how it plans to use it in an appropriate way or why it is necessary to borrow so much. However, there was not a single Minister here. I ask why would there not be a Minister introducing this legislation on behalf of the Government.
I now realize why. When you look at the Budget Papers it states the following. It states that unemployment is expected to rise in the months and years ahead. That seems to fly in the face of the arguments we heard during the last election campaign when the Government said it would be taking steps to reduce unemployment. However, the Budget indicates that unemployment levels in terms of the percentage of Canadians unemployed will actually rise in the months ahead.
It goes on to state that economic growth will slow. In other words, the economic expansion that the Conservatives promised Canadians is not going to take place. By
their own admission economic growth will be curtailed in the months ahead.
It also goes on to state that inflation will increase. We know that if inflation is going to increase-and, indeed, the Budget predicts that it will, interest rates will remain high. We know that with the current government policy of interest rates, if inflation is going to creep up, as the Budget says it will, then interest rates will increase as well.
We have to ask ourselves as Canadians why it is that we tolerate interest rates being 2.5 percentage points higher than they are in the United States when we look at the prime rates comparing one country to the other. Perhaps more telling is the rate on treasury bills with respect to which there is a 4 per cent differentiation between Canadian rates on treasury bills and American rates. Why is it that our rates are so significantly higher in Canada? Can you imagine, Madam Speaker, what that would do in terms of reducing the deficit if we simply had interest rates that were more in line with those in the United States? But the Budget says these rates will go up.
All of a sudden I begin to understand why no Minister is prepared to stand up and explain that economic growth will slow down, inflation will increase and that interest rates and unemployment are expected to rise. Why would any Minister want to do that after all of the promises made in the last election campaign?
I want to share with you two or three experiences that I have just had in the last number of days in my constituency. I visited a cattle ranch which was founded at the turn of the century. It has been in the same family now for three generations. I drove up to the ranch gate and the family was in the yard. I walked up and noticed a sense of despondency. It was very clear. Here was a family with two children, the wife worked part-time off the ranch as did the husband. This was a large cattle operation. The family complained that as a result of the high interest rates which they had to pay on a variety of loans, they were no longer able to continue operating. That day they were expecting the salesman to come to the ranch and put up a for sale sign on it. They thought I was the salesman.
June 12, 1989

Here is a third-generation cattleman. Three generations that had built, if you like, one of the most reputable operations. They were highly regarded and hard-working people in the community who worked seven long days a week who never took holidays. They could not carry on because of the Government's high interest rate policy. They asked me why the Government continued on with its high interest rate policy. Or, more important, why there were not some programs to ease the pain. In agriculture if you are paying 12 per cent, 13 per cent, 14 per cent or 15 per cent, you know, Madam Speaker, as well as I and anyone here who understands the farming business, that it is very difficult if not impossible to sustain an operation paying such high interest rates. So they are abandoning their ranch and having the usual auction sale in the weeks ahead after three generations and moving into town. That was one experience.
Then I encountered a group of tree planters driving into town who were pulling up their camp. I stopped them and talked to the group of about 15 young tree planters. They asked why the federal Government had decided not to continue on funding its reforestation programs because the Province of British Columbia was prepared to put up a substantial amount of money in that regard. However, the Province had received word that the federal Government was abandoning, in a sense, the whole matter of reforestation, Canada's No. 1 export industry which requires continuing development. These young people understood that when you cut a tree it needed replacement. As a matter of fact, three trees should be planted each time one is cut out so that over time some of the poorer plants can be culled out. They said that presumably the federal Government had decided not to fund tree planting, reforestation, thinning and spacing programs in the future and asked why. Why would that be when obviously reforestation played such a critical role in the long-term development of that No. 1 export industry of the country?.
Then I happened to drop in on an acquaintance who runs a fishing camp. This operator was at his wit's end. He had just been informed by the news media last week that the federal Government was going to impose a 9 per cent sales tax on all of the services that he provides in his fishing camp. He said, quite frankly, that if he has to add 9 per cent to his costs he cannot continue in business. He cannot continue because it is such a marginal and tight operation. It is difficult to get tourism funding these days. Essentially it is an arm of the tourist industry. He
Borrowing Authority
asked why the Government would do this when he and others are trying to employ a few people and build a critical sector for the future? Why does the Government want to impose a 9 per cent sales tax on all of the services provided.
I told him that the Government had just announced that it was not going to continue to renegotiate its tourism agreements with the provinces. He could not believe it because here was one small area where the federal and provincial governments work together encouraging the development of new tourism enterprises and the Government has announced it will not continue with the shared programs. Perhaps it will rethink this through the Western Diversification Fund although it is being cut back as well. I said I do not suppose you noticed it in the Budget but the Government has cut out a third of the tourism of Canada funding because it said there is not need now to encourage people to visit Canada. I believe, Mr. Speaker, the Government knows something which the rest of us do not.
Why encourage people to come to Canada when one of the major travel vehicles is VIA Rail. On the one hand the Government is cutting out-gutting if you like-the whole VIA program. The cynicism is evident. When you are a country like the United States and see the tourism ads, Americans are encouraging people to come to Canada and travel by VIA Rail across this great country. At the same time the Government is hacking out chunks of VIA Rail service yet using VIA Rail as a kind of incentive for people to visit Canada. The Government is cutting out tourism advertising overseas, Mr. Speaker, by reducing significantly the amount of tourism funding for federal-provincial agreements. On top of that it is slapping a 9 per cent sales tax on all services provided in that sector. As the Conference Board of Canada study said last week, Mr. Speaker, the tourism sector would be the hardest hit of the economy as a result of the new national sales tax to come into force on January 1, 1991.
I have spoken about the fishing camp operator, the tree planters and the cattleman. I could go through another list of people from last weekend's visit to the constituency who find it incredible what this federal Government is doing to them. Senior citizens have given up. There will be 128,000 senior citizens who will either have their whole old age pension or part of it clawed back. In our discussions they told me that they thought that when you reached 65 years of age you could expect the old age pension as a result of citizenship in this great

June 12, 1989
Borrowing Authority
country, that that is what it means to be a citizen of Canada. But that will no longer occur.
What has happened with this last federal Budget? Some seniors who have worked hard, and who have made investments, setting aside money during their years to provide for their retirement will not get the old age pension. It seems to be a strange motivation to us that if you work hard, save for your retirement and have some modest investments that you will not get that old age security cheque.
It is the same with family allowances. Madam Speaker. There are half a million families affected who will not get all of their family allowance cheques because they will be clawed back. All this happens at a time when tens of thousands of large profitable corporations do not pay any income tax whatever; Alcan Aluminum and Hees International to name two. Tens of thousands of profitable corporations do not pay any income tax but this Government says to old age pensioners like my dad, "we're going to claw back your pension."
People are perplexed. They do not understand why this Government is clawing back family allowances and senior citizens pensions while at the same time Hees International, Cadillac-Fairview and Alcan Aluminum pay no income tax at all in spite of hundreds of millions of dollars in profits. People cannot believe a Government would do that.
When no Minister of the Crown stands up to introduce this particular third reading stage of the debate to tell people what the Government is doing, I can understand that. I do not think I would want to stand up either. I would not want to remind people that day care had been promised especially when there are two million children who require licensed day care in Canada.
If I were the Minister of Finance I would not want to say that I knew we promised to introduce legislation to take care of that, but we are abandoning that commitment and breaking that promise. That is effectively what the Minister has said. He has said that the Government has broken the promise made to two million children
that it would provide decent child care. How crass, how cruel, how uncaring can the Government get?
The list goes on and on. I do not recall hearing the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister, when they were travelling throughout western Canada, saying that as soon as they get elected they would start abandoning support for the regions. I do not recall hearing them say that, but in this Budget that is what they have done. They have cut back on the western diversification fund and are eliminating regional development programs in both the West and the East.
lo make matters worse, the Government is cutting out many of the benefits that flow from unemployment insurance. A fisherman in an outpost of Newfoundland who fishes for a number of weeks of the year should, because of the state of the regional economy, collect unemployment insurance benefits for a number of weeks, but he will no longer be able to collect some of those benefits, and the same is true for fishermen on the West coast. There are fishermen here today who are trying to explain to the Government the realities of the regional economies. The Government is taking the fairness out of being a Canadian by cutting back on unemployment insurance support. It is cutting back on funding for western diversification and funding for Atlantic Canada.
We have heard a lot about the environment in the last little while. The Minister of the Environment and the Prime Minister say that they have now been converted into environmentalists. All of a sudden they are concerned about the environment. We must have faith in them and believe that they are telling the truth this time. I have a difficult time believing that they are telling the truth.
What did the Government do about the environment? Hon. Members will recall that the Government eliminated the Canada Oil Substitution Program. That was a program that was attempting to see that we are not so dependent on the non-renewable resource, fossil fuels. The Government cut out that program. Then it eliminated the Canadian Home Insulation Program which encouraged people to insulate their homes properly. The Government decided to remove this encouragement, and it did. Then it cut out the Canadian Energy Audit Program. Many Canadians used this program to have their homes audited to find out if they were energy
June 12. 1989

efficient. The Government cut out that program. Then it cut out the Atlantic Energy Conservation Investment Program, the Solar Energy Demonstration Program, the Remote Community Demonstration Program, the Forest Industry Renewable Energy Program, and the Industrial Conversion Assistance Program.
Of all the programs that have been developed over the last number of years to encourage conservation, the Government has virtually eliminated every single one of them. Yet, it has the audacity to say that it supports environmental issues. There is little evidence of that. The proof of the pudding is in what has been done with the environmentally sensitive programs that have been developed over the last number of years. The Government has eliminated virtually every one of them. Now I understand even better why no Minister rose to explain this program.
What about co-operative housing? Anyone who has visited or lived in a co-operative housing project knows that it has advantaged so many people and that the program is sought after by hundreds of thousands of Canadians. It enables people to live in decent accommodation at affordable prices. What has the Government's approach been to ease the housing crisis through a program that exists from coast to coast? Every major community has developed a popular, accepted and admired co-operative housing program. In its Budget the Government is reducing funding for co-operative housing. It is to be capped this year and reduced significantly in the years ahead. That option for future development and growth has been eliminated.
What are some of the ways for the federal Government to assist small businesses to expand, build new product lines, and create more employment? The Federal Business Development Bank management services have been one of the more positive aspects of the Federal Business Development Bank. There have been a number of concerns about its existing mandate as it is being interpreted, but the management services program was sought after by many people going into the small business sector, particularly those doing so for the first time. The Government announced that it would curtail these services. It said that this program offering advice and encouragement would not continue into the future.

On top of that, the Government decided that it was not necessary to maintain support for post-secondary education. We know unquestionably that the economy of the future will be knowledge and information based. It will require sophisticated skills and abilities in research and development through to production, requiring more education than ever. At such a time, the Government is starting to cut back on support for post-secondary education to the provinces.
I suppose the most discouraging aspect of this lately was the Government's decision to cap programs for young native students who want to obtain training at the post-secondary level. Can Hon. Members imagine anything more sinister than saying to young native people who are qualified and want to go on to post-secondary education that the funding will not be there? The thousands of young native people who want to go to universities, colleges, technical schools, and similar institutes will not have that opportunity because the Government is capping funding for these programs.
I see you are indicating that unfortunately my time is up. Madam Speaker. We oppose this Bill as strongly as we can. The Government that wants to borrow $24 billion is telling us that it will increase unemployment, slow economic growth, increase inflation, and keep interest rates high. At the same time, it is telling us that the deficit will actually go up next year and the year following.
I have to say that this is a Government that has not managed its affairs well. This is a Government that has no idea of where it is going. It does not know where it is taking this country. It is simply dismantling it and handing it over to the United States as a result of the trade deal. After 120 years of building, in just a few short months there has been all kinds of evidence to indicate that our country is being dismantled.
In conclusion, I want to say that Hon. Members should not be surprised when we rise in our places during the vote to oppose Bill C-ll, the Bill that would provide the Government permission to borrow $24 billion.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a few comments about the speech made by the Hon. Member and about some of the misinformation we were given about Old Age Security payments. Old Age Security payments are not being reduced and the Hon. Member knows that. He knows that Old Age Security

Borrowing Authority
payments are fully indexed and therefore will increase in future years.
The Hon. Members know that individuals receive their Old Age Security payments monthly and that they all cash their cheques without any means tests. These payments have been subject to income tax for many years. The Budget, as the Hon. Member is also aware, is using the tax system to recover payments from high income Canadians. Those measures will improve the security of our social safety net by ensuring that our social programs provide assistance to those Canadians who need it and do not subsidize high income Canadians who do not need assistance.
At the present time three million Canadians receive the Old Age Security cheques each month. Of that number 4 per cent have annual incomes in excess of $50,000. However, only 1.8 per cent of those Old Age Security recipients, those with annual incomes in excess of approximately $77,000, will pay back 100 per cent of their Old Age Security payments. One can imagine the amount of income that is needed. A person may have a large pension from work and may have $250,000, $350,000, or $500,000 in the bank in order to earn the investment income to bring their earnings up to the $77,000 limit. Perhaps the Hon. Member forgot to cover those in his notes.
I want to ask the Member a question about VIA Rail. Where would the Hon. Member get the money to cover the $600 million subsidy for VIA Rail? He gave us a travelogue when he started his address. I do not think he was travelling by train. I think that his press agent was driving him around by car.
The Member also talked about the plight of a third generation farm. It is probably a corporation. Is that one of the 80,000 corporations that did not pay tax?
VIA's ridership is 20 per cent lower than it was in 1981. From 1986 to 1988, while VIA's revenue did increase 7 per cent or some $15 million, the increase in operating cost was 10 per cent or $66 million. For every dollar of revenue that came in, the operating subsidy increased by $2.62. In other words, VIA's financial performance is worsening and not improving. I ask the Member to indicate where he would get the $600 million to cover the deficit that VIA is running.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I appreciate the questions from my hon. friend. I will attempt to answer them, perhaps in reverse order.
Was the cattle ranch that was going bankrupt one of the large corporations that did not pay any income tax? No, because it was not profitable. The 60,000 corporations to which I referred were profitable. For example, Alcan Aluminium, Hees International, and Cadillac Fairview. There are 60,000 corporations like those with profits some years in excess of $300 million that paid no income tax. No, it was not the cattle ranch, because that man was forced to sell his ranch because with the high interest rate policy he could not make any profit.
The Hon. Member asks if I support a means test. I know the Hon. Member supports a means test because he is saying if a person makes more than a certain amount, obviously he or she has the means and does not need to keep the amount of money received in old age pension cheques. I dissociate myself with that view.
There are hundreds of thousands of people from around the world who would love to be Canadian citizens, because they know that there are certain rights and privileges associated with citizenship, as well as obligations and responsibilities. As a Canadian citizen, you can send your children to high school without paying premiums or extra charges. If you are sick, you can go to the hospital and be cared for. Unlike the United States, one does not need to carry a charge card. When a citizen is aged 65, he or she is eligible for a pension.
What we are hearing from the Conservative Government is that this year it is going to claw back the pension from certain senior citizens. It is saying to certain citizens: "You made so much money you do not need a pension cheque." Next year, perhaps the Government will say to certain citizens: "You made so much money you do not need to receive medicare like the rest of Canadians, you have to take your credit card with you, your children now have their high school education paid for through the tax system," or "you have enough money so you can pay extra premiums for your children."
Where does this mentality end? Once you break what it means to be a Canadian citizen, then the whole system begins to unravel. We have to part company at this point and say that Conservatives like the idea of a means test; others of us do not. I do not suppose we can argue to
June 12, 1989

convince one or the other that we ought to change our minds on that.
I now wish to address the matter of VIA Rail. I am sure that my hon. friend did not attend any of the VIA hearings that were held across Canada. If he had attended those hearings, he could have listened to the dozens of experts on all aspects of passenger rail service. They indicated if an enterprise is to succeed, there has to be investment capital to allow it to succeed. If one wants to curtail operations, then do what the Government has done.
When the present Deputy Prime Minister was Minister of Transport, I remember him stating in the House that we can make VIA Rail a viable enterprise. We can make VIA Rail the most exciting transportation system in the world. I remember the speeches time after time of how committed he said his Government would be to develop VIA Rail properly. That would require the proper investment in infrastructure. There has to be decent cars, decent tracks, a decent relationship between CN and CP, and a decent ticketing system. In other words, provide the resources to allow VIA to do the job.
I do not know if my hon. friend has ever ridden on VIA Rail. If he had ridden on VIA Rail, he would know that the frustration that exists with the people who work for VIA is unbelievable. They cannot do the job they know they could do because they have been hamstrung, the resources have been held back, and they have to offer a mediocre service in most parts of the country. Of course, for understandable reasons then, people do not take advantage of it.
As any good business person knows, to be successful there have to be the appropriate investments. The Deputy Prime Minister and previous Minister of Transport knows full well what those investments are. He spent hours articulating them for the previous Liberal Government. He spent hours and hours indicating what had to be done to make VIA a financial success. Then the players changed. The Liberals went to the opposition benches, and the Conservatives went to the government benches, and nothing happened. As a matter of fact, it worsened. There were cuts, cuts, and cuts. It is not
Borrowing Authority
surprising that today we find VIA Rail in obviously very serious economic and financial difficulty.
Over the weekend we had the benefit of listening to Dr. Kenneth Hare. He spoke publicly on the environmental implications of eliminating much of VIA Rail passenger service. He pointed out that, particularly in the heavy corridor of central Canada from Windsor to Quebec City, if good passenger rail service is eliminated in that corridor, it is the only transportation system that is virtually guaranteed against the weather. In terms of future environmental problems, we should be developing a modern, first-class transportation passenger service in that corridor. One of the most eminent scientists on environmental matters that this country has ever seen was arguing that the Government should not proceed with its plans to dismantle VIA.
I do not know if I have answered the questions of my hon. friend adequately. In terms of a summary, no, the ranch was not a profitable corporation that was not paying income tax because it had gone out of business. Yes, I do not believe in a means test for senior citizens' pensions. Give VIA Rail the tools to do the job, give it the time, and, I use the words of the Deputy Prime Minister, "it would serve us well." Other than those points, I do not think I can add much more to the questions of the Hon. Member.
