Just let me get to that. I am of the opinion that there are times when the national good overcomes any international institutions.
In this case, I can show you where the Americans can talk with one voice about how good the GATT is and how poor the GATT is on the other side. GATT ruled and the Government succumbed. It lifted the prohibition on the exporting of unprocessed whole fish to the United States. Then our federal Government decided that it would at least not offend the GATT by putting in the landing requirement, that is, that the fishermen who caught the fish at least had to land them in Canada.
On the East Coast we are very lucky. In the Free Trade Agreement it is grandfathered that the fish in the inshore must be landed in a Canadian port. However, on
the West Coast that is what they are presently arguing with the United States. The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), who speaks for fish and trade, says that we must land the salmon in B.C. for purposes of management and conservation of our stocks. The United States is arguing that point.
I say to you, Madam Speaker, and to the government back-benchers over there who want to laugh at some of the problems of Canada that I have recently seen the American Government use the Omnibus Trade Bill against hogs in Canada being exported to the United States. They used this section to impose a countervail on the hog industry. The Americans would not wait for GATT, that was seized with looking at all agricultural subsidies in our international trade. The United States has agreed to wait for that, as has Canada, under the Free Trade Agreement. They could not wait until the Uruguay Round under GATT for the multi-trade negotiations to have analysed at least what was a subsidy within the international agriculture community. The Americans used that Omnibus Trade bill, the one which we thought before the Free Trade Agreement would never be used against Canada. The Americans used it unilaterally, without any discussions, to put a countervail on the hog industry.
The subsidy happens to come right down to the amount of the stabilization program payment to the hog producers. It is just a coincidence. It tears apart our whole stabilization program in agriculture in one decision in the United States that they would not wait for GATT. They would not even send it to the new subsidy committee, if the co-chairman has been picked for Canada. All the other officials and the mechanism are there to study subsidies over the next five year to seven years. They just did it unilaterally. Bingo. By the middle of July we will know whether it stays on or not.
All this Government is asking for is: "Tell us the means by which it got to a countervail. Tell us how you did that." It used to be they had to look at damage. They had to look and see if there was a subsidy first and then damage. Not now. The Omnibus Trade Bill has been used. It has been used against a friendly trading partner who just entered into a free trade agreement with the United States. It has been used against us.
June 12. 1989

We see from the coalition of fishermen and fish workers who have come from the West Coast that the Government cannot even put on a regulation without it being challenged, again by the United States, a landing requirement to manage and conserve the stocks within our 200-mile limit over which we have jurisdiction. That is what our trading partners are doing in our natural resources on the West Coast.
When are we going to say to National Sea or to Nova Scotians that they cannot send those 4,400 metric tons that National Sea sent over to the United States unprocessed last year will that be in violation? What will that violate? Let me explain it clearly.
We can presently send unprocessed fish because there is no regulation which says not to send. This is a year of crisis in the fisheries on the East Coast because there is no groundfish. If the federal Government decided to say that we are not going to send our groundfish whole, unprocessed, to the United States, then again it would be in violation because the U.S. would go back to the GATT.
I say to the gentleman over there that I am for anything that protects our natural resources and anything that stops that type of exploitation by the Americans against the most unprotected areas in Canada. Those areas are not run by multinationals. The fisheries is strictly a Canadian fishery, and we certainly should be able to say whether we will process here or not our fish to the finished point. Yes, if it means taking a ban against sending whole fish to the United States, I agree with it.
I certainly hope that the government will listen to the concerns of this west coast group because it is going to happen continually across our great country that our industry is going to be eroded because it hurts some aspect of the United States. They do not even have the decency to wait for the mechanism of the Free Trade Agreement to come into place or, as we have seen in the hog industry, for the GATT negotiations in Uruguay to finish.
The group that we met with today say that "Canada is the world's largest fish exporter but 4,000 B.C. shore workers and an equal number of Maritime workers face lay-offs while unprocessed fish moves south. Our greatest export industry, the mainstay of our coastal economies, is at stake if we fail to act."

subtopic: MINES AND MINING
MINES AND MINING
subsubtopic: MINERS' MEMORIAL DAY IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1937 George Orwell vividly described the life of a coal miner in these words: "In the western world the coal miner is second in importance only to the man who ploughs soil".
He went on to say that most of the things one imagines in hell are there; heat, noise, confusion, darkness, foul air and, above all, unbearably cramped space.
Yesterday, June 11, 1989, was Miners' Memorial Day in Cape Breton. We are reminded of the important role coal mining has played in the history of Cape Breton. Although many mining methods have changed since Orwell's time, the unique character of the miner, the courage and strength that Orwell so well described, have not.
The devastating fire at No. 26 colliery in Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, brings home once again just how dangerous a profession coal mining is and how the people of Cape Breton have continually had to struggle against adversity. As we turn back the pages of history we remember the tragic loss of 69 men in 1917 in the methane gas

June 12. 1989
explosion which took place in the Lingan mine, and the explosion in 1979 in Glace Bay. We especially remember the origins of Miners' Memorial Day which arose from a six year series of protests culminating in the strike of 1925 and the death of William Davis.
We can be proud of the coal mining tradition of Cape Breton and at this time we remember the contributions of all miners and all their families and above all, we honour those who lost their lives in those tragic accidents.

VIA RAIL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hundreds of constituents in my riding of Northumberland have presented me with petitions and briefs on how the Conservative Government's cuts to VIA passenger rail service will adversely affect our community. Affordable housing and a better quality of life depend on the growth of non-metropolis areas and VIA Rail is fundamental to such growth and development.
In 1988, over 160,000 passenger rail trips originated and ended at the three Northumberland station stops of Port Hope, Cobourg, and Trenton Junction.

They were informed that the Minister is unwilling to meet with community groups.
Canada's transportation system is a necessity to my riding, to Peterborough and to the nation. By refusing to consult with communities, once again we see the Government's disregard for the democratic process.
The constituents of Northumberland, of Peterborough and across Canada, depend on VIA Rail. We cannot allow this necessary service to become derailed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday Canada lost another of its great heroes. Charles Rutherford, the last remaining Canadian Victoria Cross winner from the First World War, died at the age of 97.
Mr. Rutherford was awarded the Victoria Cross, the Commonwealth's top award for gallantry, for his actions in France in August, 1918. The young Lieutenant with the Fifth Battalion of the Canadian Mounted Rifles first took on three enemy machine gun crews. That accomplished, he then attacked a pill box containing a Lewis gun section. In all, he took 80 prisoners.
Today's story about him tell us that Mr. Rutherford never talked about being a hero. He was just relieved to have survived the horror that was the First World War.
June 12, 1989

But he was a hero, one of 70 Canadians who were awarded the Victoria Cross in the First World War. They were an inspiration for a nation, the individual standouts in a Canadian force that won so much honour in the First World War.
It has been said that Canada was born as a nation during 1914 to 1918. If so, then we were very blessed in having founding fathers such as Charles Rutherford, V.C.
Our sympathy goes out to his children, grandchildren and great grandchildren.
Hear, hear!

subtopic: PLIGHT OF REFUGEES
PLIGHT OF REFUGEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Government is throwing real refugees back into their land of persecution and obstructing justice before the Supreme Court of Canada.
On January 3, the Canadian Council of Churches asked the Supreme Court to declare that the newly amended Immigration Act denies the legal rights of refugees in Canada by violating the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Bill of Rights. The churches' brief shows how 88 sections of the Immigration Act limit or deny a person's right to counsel, subject certain classes of people to cruel and unusual punishment, fail to provide fair refugee hearings, or fail to protect refugees' life, liberty and security of person.
A consensus of constitutional law experts in Canada made these same objections to the House of Commons and the Senate, but the Government refused to answer with any defence.
Now this Government refuses to give any defence before the Supreme Court. Instead, it asked the Supreme Court to deny the Council of Churches the right to be heard in court. On April 26, Judge Rouleau threw out all the Government's frivolous and deceitful arguments and ordered this Government to file its defence in 10 days. Forty seven days later, the Government still refuses to file its defence and cynically appeals Judge Rouleau's decision. Also, it hurries to deport more hundreds of refugees under this unjust and unconstitutional law. Shame on the Government.

subtopic: INITIATIVES FOR IMPROVING RACE RELATIONS
INITIATIVES FOR IMPROVING RACE RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday in Vancouver, the Hon. Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship (Mr. Weiner), announced three major initiatives aimed at promoting improved race relationships in Canada. The first will provide funding for the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police for a 10 week summer intern training project in Vancouver for 10 visible minority youth to familiarize themselves with the various facets of police work.
The second project involves commissioning Internal Briefing Associates of Vancouver to develop a national action plan for measures leading to improved relations between the police force and minority groups. This will be developed in close consultation with the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, its police minority liaison committee, the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) and other policing officials. This project will be discussed at the next meeting of federal, provincial and territorial Ministers responsible for human rights in March, 1990.
Finally, the federal Government will provide financial support to the city of Vancouver to establish the Hastings Institute, a training centre aimed at helping local organizations deal with rapid social and workplace changes. Let us all support these bold initiatives to promote unity and equality among all Canadians.

subtopic: U.S. GOVERNMENT ANTI-POLLUTION PROPOSALS
U.S. GOVERNMENT ANTI-POLLUTION PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as an MP from Atlantic Canada, I applaud the tough anti-pollution proposals being signed by President George Bush which will result in some of the toughest rules ever in the U.S. Clean Air Act. It has taken extensive efforts on behalf of all eastern premiers, New England governors, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and a new co-operative attitude in Washington to achieve this significant step.

OLDMAN RIVER DAM PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also would like to bring to the attention of the House the very serious problem of the Oldman River dam project in southern Alberta.
As in the case of the Rafferty Dam in Saskatchewan, the Alberta Government has made very little effort to assess the impact of this dam on the local economy, the local Peigan people and on the environment generally. The dam will destroy a very precious resource, the pristine wild Oldman River. The dam will destroy wildlife, marshland, fishery habitat, cottonwood forest and archaeological sites.
The federal Government must become more active and more involved regarding the questions concerning native relationships with this valley, including the rights guaranteed to the Peigan people in Treaty No. 7.
Environment Canada should provide important documentation to the organization. Friends of the Oldman River, and ensure adequate public hearings take place into this dam project. This dam issue provides the federal Government with an opportunity to go beyond rhetoric and demonstrate a commitment to environmental issues by demanding a full environment and cultural impact assessment of the dam project.
Let this Oldman River just keep rolling along.

relatives from abroad so that they can be reunited quickly in this country?

I would welcome suggestions as to practical ways in which we can make the United Nations effective in influencing the attitudes of the Chinese Government from this point
June 12. 1989

forward. I give the Member my undertaking that we will consider seriously all suggestions of that kind.

GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important for the Minister to say more about what he envisions these other agencies of the UN doing. Obviously there is a large degree of concern among Canadians in general but particularly within the Chinese Canadian community.
If there will not be a call for a debate at the Security Council regardless of whether or not that call would be vetoed, just what does the Government have in mind? speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION

One of the reasons I am calling our ambassador home for consultations is that I think it would be very important for him, for Members of this House, and for other Canadians who are interested in and knowledgeable about China to turn our minds to actions that we can take now, either as Canada or as a member of the United Nations, in trying to effect the course of events from this point forward in China.

speechtext:

and have enacted regulations that will give us proper management control over the British Columbia salmon fishery and will enable the Government to administer and manage the B.C. salmon fishery properly through these new conservation and management controls. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada is a member of the GATT. We are not proposing to leave the GATT. We propose to observe the fair trading rules that the international organization known as the GATT binds all its members to. We are now engaged in an intricate trading negotiation known as the Uruguay Round with the full support of Parties opposite, and so we must comply with the GATT.
We think the regulations we now have in place are consistent with the GATT and will enable the B.C. salmon fishery to be properly managed and controlled. That, as it is, has been challenged by the United States. We are now going before a panel under the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement which will look at these regulations to see whether or not the panel finds them consistent with the GATT. speechtext:

Motion No. 5
That Bill C-2 be amended in Clause 4 by striking out lines 10 to 13 at page 6 and substituting the following therefor:
"as full-time members persons who, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, after consultation with members of the transportation industry, are knowledgeable about one or more of the following modes of transport
(a)	air transportation
(b)	marine transportation
(c)	rail and commodity pipeline transportation."
He said: Madam Speaker, my experience in transportation both before and after becoming a Member of this House has caused me, along with others, to raise a lot of concern about the ability of members of various boards and commissions to take on that responsibility. We believe there should be at least some provision to ensure that there are board members who have at least some if not complete expertise in each field of transportation accident investigation and safety covered by this legislation.
This will ensure that when a director of investigation makes his or her report to the board there will be at least one person there who is knowledgeable in that field. I am not submitting that we could not get individuals from other sectors of our community, such as the business community, the trade union movement, universities or even from consumers' associations or some individual
Accident Investigation
citizen who has taken many years of interest in transportation matters. Of course we can get someone like that. But this amendment tries to ensure that at least some of them will have some expertise.
We also want the appointment of the Governor in Council to be made after consultation with various organizations, transportation companies and transportation unions. I think of the Centre for Guided Ground Transportation at Queen's University, Transport 2000 and of the Canadian Association of Consumers. After consulting with that wide range I would hope that they would appoint members-and I am not submitting that it should be all of them, but at least some members who come out in one form or another from the transportation industry-who are knowledgeable, not even experts but knowledgeable about one or more of modes of transportation, air transportation, marine, rail and pipeline.
I have seen too many times-in fact we just had one recently when we got the Budget and the cuts to VIA Rail. Was it the Department of Transport and transportation experts who made the submissions on what should be in the Budget about VIA Rail? No, Madam Speaker. It was the gnomes in the nether regions of the Department of Finance, who would not know one end of a locomotive from the other.
There was no knowledgeability or expertise on transportation, and particularly on rail passenger transportation, that went into the decision-making about what would be in the Budget on VIA Rail. Even more ridiculous, as I remember a famous appointment of a person to the board of directors of Air Canada, an alderperson in a city in Canada. When asked what expertise, knowledgeability the person could bring to the board of directors of Air Canada, the person said: "Well, I have flown several times." That ain't good enough. That is just not good enough. If the person had been knowledgeable about air transportation and the operation of airlines from the perspective of The Consumers Association of Canada, fine. But to pick out a citizen for other reasons than knowledgeability of Air Canada's operations, mostly political reasons if not entirely, is surely no way to subject a board or a commission with that kind of personnel on its board.
We have had the same thing happen with Canadian National. That has been one of the problems, particularly with rail transportation in Canada, CN, CP and VIA. The decision-making has been done mainly by corporation lawyers and chartered accountants and very few practising, practical railroaders, whether it was on a

June 12, 1989
Accident Investigation
board of directors, whether it was in the Department of Transport, Department of Finance or anywhere else.
That is what this amendment seeks to do. It could be an appointment of a good Conservative, a good Liberal or a good NDPer, but provided he had some knowledge and at least a minimal amount of expertise in one or more of these modes of transportation.
I have had some bitter experiences in hearings before the CTC with commissioners questioning us or trying to cross-examine us who knew absolutely nothing about what we were talking about. They were relying on their own legal and accounting staff. That is most frustrating. They did not really know. They had never been there on the ground themselves. In fact, as the farmer said: "They never had any manure on their boots." They had never been there.
When you go in front of a board or a commission with the knowledge that those are the kind of people who are going to hear you out, and know not what you are talking about, it is pretty frustrating. I submit it is very unfair, both to the board as a whole and certainly to the people of Canada. We dealt with this at some length and heard from numerous witnesses in the Transport Committee when we held hearings and when we dealt with the Bill clause by clause. Many witnesses wanted this to be the case. Some did not. Some did not think it was necessary.
I recall most of the witnesses who appeared from all sectors in transportation thought that that should be in the criteria for the appointing of members to the board. I hope that my colleagues will agree. My amendment does not go to the length where it has to be someone who is a real expert with credentials as long as your arm. When we say knowledgeable, that is a word used by the Government in an earlier section of the Bill. It is somebody who has some reasonable, however modest, knowledge about one or more of the modes of transportation that this board will deal with. Surely that is not unreasonable. I do not want to see a board with four out of five, as they say in the railroad, who could not find their backsides in the dark if they used both hands, when it comes to transportation.
I am trying to safeguard that because of the previous experiences I have had, as have many others who have complained to me and to the Government. Certainly the media has, when they looked at the qualifications of appointments made by the government of the day. This is a small and modest attempt to correct previous practice.

Madam Speaker, I rise to support the amendment proposed by my colleague, the Member for Regina- Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin). There is no question that the amendment put forward by my colleague is an important amendment. In fact, I would submit it is fundamental to the Bill. Members of the House should be aware that what this accident investigation and safety board will do is replace all other accident investigation boards currently at work for the Government of Canada and on behalf of the people of Canada.
For the moment, we have accident investigators operating independently in the air mode, in the marine mode and in the railroad. Of course, the pipeline mode is handled by the National Energy Board. What we are proposing is to consolidate all of those accident investigators in one body and one authority. Whereas for the moment we have perhaps two or three dozen boards made up of two or three dozen board members, what this new Bill will do is just give us five board members for all modes. Hence, the title multi-modal agency. In that instance it becomes not only important but critical that the board members who are appointed not only enjoy the confidence of the Government in the normal way but also have a level of expertise in at least one of the modes covered by a multimodal agency.
We will be proposing a little later this afternoon an amendment to Clause 12. In that amendment dealing with quorums we are asking that a quorum shall be not only three to five members but that at least one of the three must have some expertise in the area of transportation occurrence that is being discussed. It goes without saying that unless there is a guarantee of expertise to begin with-hence the motion of the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin)-it is pretty difficult for the latter amendment that we have put to have any meaning.
June 12, 1989

On this side of the House we certainly embrace the notion that the Government, that is, the Cabinet, ought to be directed in this legislation to ensure by legislative requirement that the people who are given these jobs for a period of seven years be not just people who enjoy the confidence of Cabinet but who, after consultation with the transportation industry, are appointed on the basis of recognized and demonstrated expertise. The period of seven years came about as a result of an amendment made in committee.
One would hope-in fact, one would expect-that whether or not this amendment is in the Bill, this Government or any other Government would make appointments of individuals who have that kind of expertise. However, if it is the expectation of all Members that board members will have expertise and will not merely be friends of the Government of the day of whatever stripe, then let us put it in the Bill. Let us ensure that the people who answer ultimately to Parliament and on behalf of all Canadians for the operation of the multimodal accident investigation board are people who are there as a consequence of their expertise and for no other reason.
I submit that given the history of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, given the general level of lack of confidence by the public in that board because of the controversy and split in the board over Gander, it is more important now than ever before that we not only assure Canadians of a qualified board but that we demonstrate it by insisting upon those qualifications in the Bill.

May I say this about Motion No. 6. The main thing this motion is trying to secure is that the chairman of the Canadian Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board will not have powers delegated to him by the Governor in Council and the Minister of Transport which make that chairperson of the Board a czar, one who can do almost anything he or she wants to do in exercising that supreme authority bestowedby the Governor in Council and the Minister of Transport by regulation.
Surely the fundamental principle of a board is its collectivity, that a decision is by the board and not by somebody outside the board. It is sufficient that the Minister has the prerogative to choose and appoint a chairman. Except for what is in this Bill, surely all other authorities and rules have to be decided by the board as a whole. The chairperson of the board will be governed by those rules, will work within that framework and not be a
Accident Investigation
czar with the rest of the board members merely rubber stamps. There must be a collectivity of the entire board in the devising of the rules of the operations, the rules of investigation, rules regarding the allocation of duties and what not. Without that you end up with one or more rubber stamps on the board.
In relying on some of my own experience years ago appearing before the Canadian Transport Commission, the chairman of the Commission had supreme authority over all members of the Board. I can recall one occasion when we were dealing with transcontinental passenger trains as they were then operated or not operated by CN and CP. A group of three witnesses appeared before the Commission in Regina. The chairman kept interrupting the witnesses, commenting and editorializing on what was in their submission.

decision of the entire board, a frame of reference under which the chairman must act.
It seems to me that what this amendment seeks to do is so obvious that there should be no difficulty having it accepted. In exercising the powers given to him by the board, the chairperson of the board still has to take into account other laws that affect the operations of the board, including the Public Service Employment Administration Act, the Public Service Staff Relations Board legislation, the Canada Labour Code and a whole host of other laws by which not only the chairperson but the members of the board will be governed. Madam Speaker, I rise to support my motion, motion No. 7, and I compliment my colleague from Regina on his remarks about motion No. 6. That motion is very similar in content and intent.
I suggest that fundamentally what my colleague from Regina is attempting to do and what I am attempting to do today through this motion is to make the wording of the Bill more simple than it is at the present. I agree with the Hon. Member that during the committee meetings,
at which we heard many witnesses, one of the fundamental concerns about this Bill was with regard to the dispute under the previous legislation, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board Act, as to what the duties of the chairman were or ought to have been and what the duties of the board members were or ought to have been. When we reviewed that legislation, we found that there was some fuzziness and that there was no clear intention given to either one or the other as to what its duties and functions were to be.
My colleagues and I, including the Conservative members of the committee whom I compliment for this, were all trying during our deliberations to come up with something that was workable for this clause of the Bill to allow the chairman to pursue his duties without confrontation with board members and for the board members to perform their duties without confrontation with the chairman, something which I am sure both sides wanted to do under the old legislation. That is what we are attempting to do by moving these motions in the committee.
For clarification and for the benefit of my friends across the Chamber, let me deal with motion No. 7, which is fairly simple. The motion provides that the chairperson is the chief executive officer of the board. Let us deal with the concept of a chief executive officer. How would that be interpreted in a court of law? We are trying, for the sake of clarity, to avoid the kind of confrontation that may occur in the courts if certain clauses of the Bill are taken for interpretation.
I think it is implicit to any of us in this room or to any court that a chief executive officer has extra duties over and above those of a general manager or a chairman of the board. The chief executive officer of any corporation, if we make this analogous to a corporation, has many added duties. Many committees report to the chief executive officer about ongoing activities of the board over which he is the chief executive officer.
We often talk about the president of an organization together with the chief executive officer, but they are separate titles. In this legislation, we are saying that the chairperson shall be the chief executive officer. I think it goes without saying that it is still left for the Minister responsible to make that appointment, and we are not debating that, although there was some discussion about it. If I am correct, the appointment of a member from the five-member board was to come from one who was
June 12, 1989

extremely knowledgeable in administrative matters as they affect public institutional boards.
By calling the chairperson the chief executive officer, the Bill already gives that person substantial powers. We are not trying to take these powers away from the board but from the chairman so that they are vested in the board. We are asking our friends to consider taking away from the Bill the reference to managing personnel matters, financial matters and property matters and all other aspects of the internal management of the board. It is our hope that these activities become the responsibility of the board which in turn, through powers given to it later on in the Bill, can delegate them to those responsible should the board decide that these administrative matters or personnel matters should be delegated. It has the power to delegate them and it can delegate those powers to the chief executive officer or to the general manager.
The fundamental point is that once those powers are delegated, rather than coming back to the chairperson, those matters have to be reported back to the board in its entirety, the chairperson be part of the board. It is a board responsibility for the administration of those affairs and the administration of the Act.
With respect to my colleague from Regina-I know that this is the position of our members-by delineating those substantial powers, not removing them from the structure of the committee but removing them from the chairperson's responsibility and putting those functions into the board's responsibility, whoever is fulfilling those functions must report back to the board, it would go a long way to correcting the problems that, in our opinion, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board had in the administration of its affairs, particularly when it came to the investigation of accidents.
That is the fundamental reason why we discussed at great length the differences in the delineation of powers between the chairperson and the members of the board. It is our position that the board should retain those powers. I hope that my friends and colleagues across the aisle will reconsider their position on that point, see the
Accident Investigation
wisdom of our deliberations and our investigation into this area and grant us this motion.

Madam Speaker, Motions Nos. 6 and 7 that we are debating today spring from the same general concern over the concentration of power in the chairperson of the board. The feeling of members of the Opposition is that the Government would be well advised to consider amendments which distribute this power in a way that would make the board more of a collective decision-making body in reality and in practice.
The concern with the amount of power vested in the chairperson by the legislation as we have it now without those amendments, is that there will be a tendency on the part of board members, staff, and everyone, as has been the case before with other boards, to defer to the judgment, to the desires, biases, prejudices, however one wants to describe it, of the chairperson. In the final analysis, this is destructive of the collegiality and the collective decision-making that we want the board to be capable of. The Liberal amendment and our amendment, both from two different angles, address that problem.
The Conservative Government has a history of talking about the decentralization of power and not wanting to vest any one bureaucrat with too much authority. Here it has an opportunity to live up to its own rhetoric. What is it doing? It is going down the same old Liberal bureaucratic road of vesting all the power in one appointee who no doubt will know very little about that which he is appointed to preside over. He might be somebody rescued from a parliamentary debacle, such as Mr. Nielsen was when he was appointed to the NTA, and there are numerous other examples. I realize that this is an ad hominem argument. However, given those types of people, and the type of authority that this legislation does give, it is an invitation to tyranny which should be repudiated by Parliament.

subtopic: CANADIAN TRANSPORTATION ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION AND SAFETY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to support the motion of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Comuzzi), and by extension to support the motion of the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin).

June 12, 1989
Accident Investigation
These amendments provide an opportunity for the House to make a straightforward but fundamentally important decision. The decision is, I believe, the crux of the whole debate that we have had in the Standing Committee about this Bill. I submit that the cleanest of the two amendments is the one presented by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Comuzzi). However, without one of those amendments, simply put, the new multi-modal accident investigation board will be run by a chairman. As the Bill is currently drafted, the chairman of the board will have all financial power, all powers of delegation, will have the power to hire and fire the chief investigators into major transportation accidents or occurrences, will have the power to set the agenda of the board, and will have the power to decide what board members will do what work. In essence, one individual will have all of the legislative authority required to literally completely run an agency with the responsibility for doing an overview or an investigation of four modes of transportation. That is a tremendous amount of power to put into the hands of one individual.
The other four board members of this multi-modal agency will only be able to function at the discretion of the chairman, and to the extent that the chairman shall allow them to function as independent agents exercising their best judgment and consciences in, first, conducting investigations, and second, reporting to the public on causes of major transportation accidents.
These amendments propose to acknowledge a board of five individuals. Hopefully, they will be individuals qualified for this type of work.
However, as the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon proposes, it leaves it to the board, to five, mature, intelligent, dedicated, and qualified men and women to establish for themselves ground rules as to how they will function, to establish for themselves collectively what type of accidents ought to be investigated and in what manner they should be investigated. It also leaves them to establish for themselves what kind of qualified staff should work on behalf of this board and should have the power collectively to hire and fire.
The question is a very fundamental one. Given the history of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board, the history of division, the current lack of public confidence
that arose out of dissent, do we respond to what was too much dissent that caused a loss of public credibility in the case of CASB and the Gander crash, and the tragic loss of life, by totally eliminating the possibility of dissent? By having a chairman with an iron fist? By ensuring that members, even if they disagree in the most fundamental way with the workings of the board or the conclusions of an accident investigator, are silenced by cutting off their hands or by sealing their lips? Does one respond to dissent by ensuring that there is never dissent again?
Not one single witness who came before our committee suggested, nor would any serious individual suggest, that dissent of and by itself is a bad thing. That is why there is more than one member of a board, because more than one point of view is wanted, and the possibility of a minority or a majority disagreeing with the conclusions or practices of a chairman. That is the very essence of democracy. That is what this Chamber is about. It is a vehicle for dissent in a democratic society.
It seems strange to me that Parliament would concoct, as important as it is, an agency called the multi-modal accident investigation agency and establish it in a way that would eliminate the fundamental of any reputable agency, that is, that there is the possibility of dissent.
That there is the possibility of more than one point of view being heard so that as we sail Canada's waters, as we fly, through jet aircraft or other means, Canada's skies, as we take the rails across this country, as we sit in our seats and travel, we can rest assured that there is a multi-modal agency that has within it a board that has the power of dissent, the ability for more than one opinion, and the most critical analysis possible to ensure safe transportation.
Failure to adopt the amendment by my friend, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Comuzzi), or the amendment of the Hon. Member for Regina- Lumsden (Mr. Benjamin), leaves us with a possible situation. I am not saying it is certain, but it is certainly possible that one strong-willed chairman will run this board in such a way that it will be the brainchild, the baby, a vehicle for the thoughts and views of only one person and that four other people will act as mere window dressing. As I fly along, as I frequently do back and forth to Newfoundland, I do not find that a comfort-
June 12, 1989

ing thought. I do not believe that Canadians would find it a comforting thought.
If we are not afraid of more than a single point of view being heard on something as fundamental as safety in transportation, let us create a board that is truly a collective board with collective authority. Let us not establish a board with a chairman who reigns supreme, because we know from experience throughout history that that kind of configuration, whether it be for political purposes or in the workings of any kind of committee, leads not to a healthy, open and democratic institution but, rather, to an institution that too frequently ends up resembling the views of one individual. That is not in the interests of Canadians.

Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-St. Barbe -Baie Verte)
moves:
Motion No. 8
That Bill C-2 be amended in Clause 12 by adding immediately after line 12 at page 11 the following:
"(3) At meetings of the Board convened for the purpose of discussing a specific transportation occurrence, at least one member of the Board shall be qualified in the mode of transportation which is the subject matter of the occurrence."
Accident Investigation
He said: Madam Speaker, I want to say at the outset in proposing this amendment to colleagues opposite, who are no doubt sitting on the edges of their seat waiting to hear the rationale for this important motion, that I make a genuine appeal to Members to consider the value of this amendment. I should say for Members who are here in the House today but who were not part of the work of the standing committee, that I believe the work of the Standing Committee on Transport on this Bill reflected perhaps more than the work of any other committee in my memory and time here the spirit of reform as proposed by the McGrath-Ouellet-Blaikie committee.
Madam Speaker, I refer to Members' names only in the context of the reform report because what that committee proposed was that in so far as the deliberations of Members are concerned with respect to creating legislation in standing committees-not here in the House, not before television cameras, not in the context of a partisan exchange in an election, not even in the context of Question Period, but in the context of individual Members with an interest in a particular area, in this case transportation-that we really ought to be not Liberals, New Democrats or Conservatives but individual Members exercising their best judgment. That is what the spirit of reform was all about.
In the standing committee, we saw many occasions where both Liberal, New Democrat and Conservative Members disagreed with the Party line. We saw motions proposed by the Opposition defeated, motions that we thought would have carried because they had government support, but because opposition Members did not agree. We saw government motions defeated or opposition Members carried with the support of government Members. It happened repeatedly. The exercise in the standing committee consequently was a very good exercise, not only for Members but for Canadians. They got a non-partisan effort.
I say that because I want Members who were not part of the standing committee to look at the amendments we are proposing in the same light. The amendment. Motion No. 8, proposes to change Clause 12, which essentially sets out the size of the quorum. It states three Members constitute a quorum. We want to add to that by saying that at meetings of the Board convened for the purpose of discussing a specific transportation occurrence-that means an accident-at least one member of the board shall be qualified in the mode of transporta-

June 12, 1989
Accident Investigation
tion which is the subject matter of the occurrence. In other words, if three members come together to discuss an aviation disaster-God forbid-three out of five, that one of those three must be somebody with aviation experience. It could not be more obvious than that.
If there were an accident on the pipeline side such as we saw in the horrific incident in Russia last week where hundreds, perhaps 1,000 lost their lives, that three of the five who get together to discuss a pipeline occurrence in Canada, one of those three must have expertise in the pipeline area. The same for rail and marine. All we are saying is that if you have a major occurrence in one of the modes, let us not have an aviation expert, a marine expert, or a rail expert discussing pipelines. Let us not have a rail expert and a marine expert, in a third mode, discussing an aviation occurrence. Let us at least require that one of the board members with knowledge and expertise other than the full-time bureaucracy must be qualified to discuss an event.
It seems such an obvious and rational approach to doing the business of the board that it should not require amendment. But I believe it does require an amendment. Everyone would tell us, if Members opposite would stand and speak, that they would not disagree with that. They expect that is the way the board is going to work anyway. It is such a logical thing that no one could disagree. If that is the case, let us put it in the Bill. Let us rest assured that when the board considers a tragic occurrence-and a tragic occurrence translates into loss of life, such as Gander, Dryden, Hibernia oil disaster, to name but three-the job of the board is twofold. It should investigate, tell us what went wrong, and make recommendations so that those kinds of occurrences may never happen again.
Surely, Members using free will and concerned only with making a better Bill, should not be concerned with whether the motion comes from a Liberal, a New Democrat or a Conservative, but concerned only with creating the best legislation possible. They could not disagree with what is such a humble but fundamental proposition necessary to ensure that this Bill is a good Bill, that Parliament has done its job and that the people of Canada are well served.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to compliment the Hon. Member for the amendment he has moved. The Hon. Member's motion is in some ways a consequence of my Motion No. 5 on which the vote has been deferred, but can also stand on its own no matter what happens with that vote.
According to the Bill as it reads now, people can be appointed to the board because they belong to the frequent flyer plan. People can be appointed for being a frequent ferry user, a frequent shipper and receiver of freight, a frequent passenger on VIA Rail for however long it lasts. That is not good enough.
The motion would require that there be some qualification for one of the modes of transportation under which the investigation of an occurrence is taking place. Again, reflecting on our experience with previous boards and commissions, one cannot have a chartered accountant deciding what happened in a railway wreck no more than a locomotive engineer, trainman or dispatcher can decide on accounting law. This is so self-evident that I wish the Parliamentary Secretary would get up and state whether the Government is prepared to accept these amendments. Perhaps he can give us the rationale for supporting the Bill in its present form and the reasons for rejecting this or any of the other amendments so that people can decide, in light of our arguments and his arguments, which side may have a case.
All Members will agree that the committee had an excellent session dealing with the Bill clause by clause. We heard many witnesses and dealt with them expeditiously. It was a non-partisan exercise, and there were occasions when members of the committee, from both sides of the table, agreed or disagreed with elements of the original Bill. That is how committees should function under the new regime of so-called committee independence.
The Government has not provided sufficient argument in support of this aspect of the Bill. I recall talking to a member of the former Canadian Transportation Commission who was travelling to another part of Canada to investigate a railway accident. We were on the train from Winnipeg to Regina, when we pulled into a siding. He did not know that eastbound trains had priority over westbound trains, which is a fact known to railroaders
June 12, 1989

from management to the workers on the tracks. Ele did not know that first-class trains had priority over second-class trains.
He did not even know the meaning of the green board, orange board and red board on the train ordinal signals beside the tracks. What does the amendment state? I believe that it should be reread. I would like my colleagues from the New Democratic Party to pay attention to it. It states:
An employee statement obtained pursuant to a collective agreement is privileged, and no person shall have access to such statements, except as authorized in writing by the person who made the statement.
What it states is that in the course of conducting an investigation into an incident, an occurrence, an accident, that in some modes, specifically for the moment in the rail mode, there are provisions in the collective agreement between the company and the employees which prevent statements made by employees to company officials from being made public. In other words, those statements must be kept in confidence.
Members should know that both the industry-these companies in question-and the employees in question on any number of Bills appearing before the standing committee have said that the confidential nature of those statements made by employees to their employers have become extremely important to the safe operation of train companies, that is, CN and CP.
Why is that? It is because both parties know that those statements when given will be kept in the strictest of confidence, that those statements will not find their way outside the employee-employer relationship and that employees making statements having that assurance are completely free to be forthright, honest and aboveboard.
In terms of safety, because there is a guarantee of the confidentiality of that statement, the value of the information given is multiplied 1,000 per cent in the day-today running of the company. Those employee statements are not just information on how the widgets work or on how the technology works, but are also comments on some occasions without prejudice on the performance of fellow employees. As trains hurdle across the tracks with freight and bodies-human beings aboard those trains- we know there is an employer-employee relationship providing for a frank and full exchange of information aimed at ensuring safety.
What this Bill would do unless amended would be to give the investigators the power to subpoena those confidential statements made under a provision of the collective agreement. The second this Bill has the power to subpoena those statements, you can be sure that the nature of those statements will change. Once the employee and the employer knows that those statements are liable to end up as a centrepiece to an investigation, the day-to-day practice and operation of that railroad company, based on the value of these confidential statements, is gone. You will no longer have the kind of openness and forthright comment in those confidential statements that today are a large contributor to the safe operation of the railways.
Now logically the public might say: "Well, you know, if there is an accident I want those investigators to get their hands on every piece of information available. I don't care about a collective agreement.", except you have to be aware that the day you violate the collective agreement those statements no longer have any value. In other words, the kind of material going into those statements will radically change. It will be puffery.
What I propose to do in this amendment is to protect those confidential statements which are part of the collective agreement, to protect the value that they have for the daily running of a railroad not only on the

occasion of an accident but day to day, week to week, month to month, year-in and year-out. At the same time, if you look at the wording, it says that the statements shall be protected except as authorized in writing by the person who made the statement. There is nothing stopping an employee who feels that something he has said, some information he has, is valuable to an investigation from making that information available to the Board.
The Bill goes further. What about Clause 30? An existing clause in the Bill says that any information given to the Board by an employee wanting to contribute to an investigation that that information shall be kept confidential from the company. There is already a guarantee in this Bill that if some employee, in any mode of transportation, goes to the Board independently to say: "Look, I think there is information you should have about my company, the way it operates or a fellow employee that is pertinent to an investigation", that that information shall be kept confidential. Again, it is information obtained on a voluntary basis.
If the Bill recognizes the importance of keeping information confidential through Clause 30, an employee who wants to make information available to the Board is given protection as it were, then surely this Bill should also anticipate and recognize the value of the collective agreement clause which provides for confidential statements between the employer and employee and that the value of those statements is lost the day those statements are no longer protected.
Members will well appreciate, although it seldom works as well as we would like, but the purpose of a caucus among political parties is to allow free, frank and open discussion without fear theoretically that that discussion will find itself into the front pages of the newspaper. CANADA LABOUR CODE
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Canada Labour Code to provide all regulated workers with the right to create, upon the demand of 10 or more workers, a Technological Change Committee which will be entitled to advance notice of technological change and full information about the impact of proposed technological changes on employment, job content and work processes.
He said: Madam Speaker, it gives me a great deal of satisfaction to be a participant in what I understand to be the changed rules of the House for Private Members hour. When I submitted this motion, I had no idea that the Government would come up with a reference to training ethic, which reference occurs in the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is an admission by the Government that the corporate world has some responsibility to society and to its employees.
Training ethic does not express my entire concern insofar as the private sector is concerned. I suggest that
the right of employees to become involved in technological change as it affects them, their workplaces and their communities is an extension of the idea of the training ethic into what I think ought to be described as the total responsibility of the private sector.
Motion 225 brings to our attention the fact that the corporate world is not living up to its responsibility when it comes to the introduction of technological change in the workplace. It is not living up to its responsibilities to employees and to the communities in which it operates.
The motion provides that employees should have the right to a Technological Change Committee with the right to be informed well in advance of changes which could affect their jobs, their health, their safety, their earning capacity, the work processes with which they have to become familiar and indeed the content of their jobs themselves. I say they should be informed well in advance. I hesitate to put a time limit on it, but I would suggest that a minimum time ought to be at least 12 months. In short, the motion provides that workers be given full information about the impact of proposed technological changes on employment, job content and work processes.
Employees and the communities in which they live have a right to know well in advance of changes which, as experience has already shown, affect the employees and communities adversely in almost all cases. The situation with which we are faced is contrary to what we were told at the outset of this technological revolution. I am sure everyone here remembers the glowing terms with which the technical revolution was introduced, the stories which purveyors of new technology told us when it was being introduced into society. New technology was to create a society that would be beyond our wildest dreams, a leisure society in which everyone was able to benefit from the wealth created.
There is no doubt that more leisure time has been created. We see it almost everywhere and we see its negative face of unemployment. There can be no question that the technological changes introduced within the last decade have contributed in no small measure to the very high degree of unemployment from which society is suffering. With the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, I would suggest that the level of unemployment will be even higher and more obvious.
June 12, 1989

The wealth has been created too. Over the last decade since the major introduction of technological changes, the corporate world has experienced for the most part an even level of return on investment, but that return has not found its way down, as the monetary theories of Milton Friedman, Ronald Reagan, Margaret Thatcher and the like would have us believe. It has not trickled down to the average Canada, or for that matter, to the average person anywhere within the spheres of influence of Milton Friedman's misguided economic theory. Employees have not benefited, nor has society benefited. There are more food banks than one could have imagined at the end of the 1930s and during the economic up-turn of the 1950s and the 1960s. The communities have not benefited.
Motion 225 is an attempt to ensure that the promise of the technological revolution is fulfilled for all Canadians. To that end, it is necessary to look at some of the proposals for employment, job content and work processes in a more detailed way.
First, we must have definition of technological change. This definition must include reference to the work, the undertaking or the business carried on by an employer. It must include reference to any change in equipment or material used in the work, undertaking or business of the employer. It must include any change in the methods utilized in the work, undertaking or business of the employer and it must recognize any change in the way in which equipment or material is used in the work, undertaking or business of the employer.
If we are to protect employees as fully as they ought to be protected from the adverse effects of technological change, we need to have provisions for them to receive adequate notice of the fact that there will be a change in the workplace as defined by technological change. This is important for several reasons. The experience of industrial assistance programs have demonstrated with the more advance notice to employees of lay-offs, and there is the possibility of lay-offs when it comes to technological change and I will deal with that later, the adverse effects on the communities, on the employees and on the employers as well for that matter are far less severe than they are when, as is too often the case, the employees go to work at 8 o'clock in the morning only to be told at 8.05 that their jobs are no longer viable and that by 12 noon they must have cleaned out their lockers, taken their
Technological Change
clothes and equipment home and turned in whatever belongs to the company.
As one can imagine, under such circumstances the trauma is insurmountable. The personal loss and grievance suffered are immeasurable. Notice has to be given of contemplated changes, and that is obvious for the reasons I have already mentioned.
There has to be a disclosure by the employer of the nature and the description of the technological changes themselves. There also have to be provisions that the effect of the technological change is made available to the employees. Issues have to be raised, such as the number of employees who will be affected. In cases where a company has more than one place of operation, the location where those jobs will be affected, the job classes involved, as well as those jobs and classifications that will be terminated or redesigned in such a way that retraining may also be necessary.
The effects on employees also has to be part of the disclosure provisions for the protection of employees. For example, effects on such things as skills and whether the skills the employees have will be adequate to enable them to remain at work. Whether they will be able to exercise the skills they have, or indeed whether they may have to acquire new ones.
It is important for employees to know whether the skills and the seniority they have accrued will enable them to remain as employees of the company. There also have to be provisions to apprise the employees of the effects of the technological changes on their health and safety.
Within the terms of disclosure, it would also be helpful for employees to be able to visit locations where the proposed changes have already been put into effect in order that the committee which will be set up will be able to evaluate whether or not in the first instance the proposals the company is making are realistic, and whether or not the disclosure with which they are in the process of being involved bears relation to what is likely to happen.
An important element, and something which all parties concerned should rightfully be aware of, is the matter of confidentiality. Quite often the implication comes forth that if the company is to disclose its innermost secrets in so far as what it is going to do, the employees will spread that information, or perhaps in

June 12, 1989
Technological Change
the first instance the company will, and by definition that is foolishness. Technological change proposals should involve, quite rightly, provisions for confidentiality.
There should be assurances of job security both for those employees who will remain and for those who will be laid off or whose jobs will be significantly altered. There should be a designation in the original disclosure information put out by the company for those employees it considers will be redundant and for those employees who will no longer be able to remain. Once having made those commitments, those who have not been designated should not in any way be considered as being liable to be laid off as a result of the subsequent technological change. In no case should designated employees be let go before the implementation of the technological change, or before the effective date.
As is often mentioned in relation to workers and employees, training is absolutely essential. There have to be major provisions within the technological change language which ensures that those employees who will no longer be able to retain the jobs that they had will be retrained as a right, and if there are choices for jobs which they conceivably could exercise as a result of their seniority or skills, that they be able to exercise that choice on the basis of their own preference and where they would prefer to go. The whole matter of training is predicated on the assumption that it would be the employer that paid for the training.
There certainly are instances where employees are laid off as a result of technological change, and that has been the long-term experience of many thousands of employees in this fair country of ours. They should be able to exercise the option of taking severance in lieu of training or job guarantees. This is in the interest of the employee as well as the company, because there would be no point in the company forcing an employee to stay against his or her will. For one thing, the employee most likely would not be leaving unless he or she had found employment elsewhere. Who would want to deny them that opportunity? Within the provisions of severance there is also the matter of the employee being able to take a portion of the training allowance as severance pay.
Early retirement may also be a provision that some employees would want to exercise when it comes to the implementation of technological change. Certainly, that is something the legislation ought to take cognizance of. That would certainly be a step forward for some of the older workers within our society, and also in the context of having discussed the aids to older workers in the House within the last few weeks.
The committee itself is an integral part of the whole process. It would have to be involved in the review and resolution of such issues as the need or justification for technological change and the evaluation of the appropriate change. I would suggest that that is a wise thing to do. Often the employees on the floor are able to input knowledge into the operation which oftentimes the company itself has overlooked.
The committee would be involved in the matter of adaptation by all to the proposed changes and the impact on employees. In short, the committee would be involved in the whole process, but not to the point where it would have the final say on the resolution. There have to be realistic provisions for some type of a resolution when the company and the employees are unable to agree and the solution may possibly be that the technological change would not be implemented at all. It may also be that arbitration could be considered.
The matter of surveillance is a very important issue to address. Since my time is almost up, I would point out that as far back as 1972 the Government of Sweden enacted a law which prevented some of the most obvious surveillances. For example, the use of microtechnology to monitor workers and their actions, or as a matter of discipline.
In conclusion, I am sure reference will probably be made to the 10 employees within a company asking for those changes. Some people will say that is not a very large number of people, but I would suggest that there are many, many institutions within our society that can implement changes and initiate actions within our society and foundations with small numbers in relation to the whole.
