I see that my time has lapsed. I would conclude on the basis that I do hope the House take serious consideration of the matter of technological change and its impact on Canadian workers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ken James (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: CANADA LABOUR CODE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the motion before the House proposes that Parliament should consider amending the Canada Labour Code in order to provide all regulated workers with the right to create, upon the demand of ten or more workers, a technological change committee. This committee would be entitled to advance notice of the technological change and to full information about the impact or proposed technological changes on employment, job content and work processes.
I welcome the opportunity to speak on the motion. Technological change and the process of adjustment to change are matters of great importance to Canadians as they affect the competitiveness of our industries and the people who work in them. These issues require careful consideration and I commend the Hon. Member for having introduced the motion.
Our economic performance in the world today is of vital importance to the employment and income prospects of Canadians. It will become increasingly so in view of our need to be competitive internationally. Good industrial relations will form an important part of and make a meaningful contribution to our economic performance. For that reason, we should have an appreciation of a number of significant elements of our industrial relations system as set out in Part I of the Canada Labour Code that are pertinent to the motion before us.
The regulated industries to which the motion refers encompasses a broad range of economic and industrial activities. These are the industries covered under the jurisdiction of the Canada Labour Code which include interprovincial and international railways, airlines, interprovincial highways, transport, telephone, telegraph and cable systems, pipelines, canals, ferries, tunnels and bridges, shipping, longshoring, broadcasting, banking and the primary fishing industry. Most crown corporations are also included and certain undertakings that have been declared by Parliament to be for the general
Technological Change
advantage of Canada, including grain elevators, uranium mining and processing, and flour and feed mills.
In other words, the motion would affect a large number of industries that are interprovincial and international in character as well as being of consequence to the national economy and to our national well-being.
The motion suggests that we amend the Canada Labour Code. We should, therefore, briefly review the provisions of the Code, including what it attempts to achieve. According to the preamble to the Code, Parliament recognizes the long tradition in Canada of labour legislation and policy designed to promote the common well-being through the encouragement of free collective bargaining and the constructive settlement of disputes.
It is through its principal elements that the Code establishes collective bargaining as the means through which an efficient and equitable system of industrial relations is achieved.
What are some of the principal elements of our industrial relations system? Part I of the Canada Labour Code establishes a legislative framework of rights and responsibilities within which management and organized labour are to conduct their relations.
The Code grants a legal recognition to the bargaining relationship through the principle of freedom of association and through bargaining unit certification and voluntary recognition provisions. It provides for the settling or adjudication of industrial relations issues of a legal nature by establishing the Canada Labour Code Relations Board to oversee the administration of certain of the Code's provisions.
The Code also sets out the important dispute resolution procedures through conciliation and mediation which assist in the settlement of high profile disputes that have a direct impact on the public interest. These procedures are administered by the federal mediation and conciliation service of Labour Canada.
Investigation of disputes involves, first, collective agreements and complaints of bargaining-related unfair labour practices. These important elements of our industrial relations legislation contribute to a high degree of the stability and industrial relations in the federal jurisdiction.

June 12, 1989
Technological Change
At this point, I would like to make a few remarks about the technological change provisions in the Canada Labour Code. These provisions are not only germane to the motion brought forward by the Eton. Member, but also constitute an important element of industrial relation systems at this federal level.
The introduction of technological change can have a significant impact on individual workers in terms of income and employment effects. While the introduction of new technology may result in lay-offs and lost income, society as a whole benefits from having more productive and efficient economic assets in place.
Under the provisions of the Canada Labour Code, employee involvement in the implementation of technological change is accomplished primarily through collective bargaining. These provisions encourage unions and management to meet, discuss and reach agreement on ways to minimize the negative effects on employees of technological change. Where the parties have not made provision in their collective agreements for managing the effects of technological change on employees, then the statute provides for collective agreement in force between the parties to be reopened and those provisions relating to terms and conditions or security of employment to be renegotiated.
The board may also grant leave to a union to serve notice to commence collective bargaining. The effect of such leave is that the introduction of technological change is suspended until collective bargaining results in a new agreement or the right to strike or lock-out is required.
Labour and management are free to include in their collective agreements provisions designed to resolve and address issues related to the impact of technological change. There is nothing in the legislation to prevent the parties from establishing committees, as suggested by the motion, dealing specifically with technological change.
In general, the Code provides for measures that ensure the implementation of collective agreements and for the comprehensive and flexible system which facilitates negotiation of these agreements.
The Government has sought to encourage private sector initiatives to a much greater extent in the Canadian society and to urge less reliance on the Government in achieving economic and social goals. This approach to
government policy places a greater responsibility on management and unions to resolve their differences without government interference. This is precisely the intention of the approach the Government has taken toward labour relations issues in Canada in its support for individual initiative.
In summary, my review of the industrial relations system at the federal level has attempted to illustrate some of the more salient features or relevance to the Lion. Member's motion. In particular, the large extent to which labour and management resolve their collective bargaining differences between themselves directly attests to the appropriateness of our industrial relations policy which seeks to avoid unnecessary intervention.
In this connection, we have to question the need for the introduction of the motion to amend the Code as proposed. We have to ask whether the intervention suggested by this amendment is warranted or justified. I submit that the Lion. Member has drawn our attention to an issue of continuing concern and a matter over which we will want to maintain a watchful eye as the introduction of technological change is an ongoing process with far reaching consequences.
At this present time, I see no evidence that would warrant an amendment to the technological change provisions of the Code.

subtopic: CANADA LABOUR CODE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise today in support of the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Saskatoon-Dun-durn (Mr. Fisher). Specifically, the motion requests that the Government consider the advisability of amending the Canada Labour Code. The amendment would provide all regulated workers with the right to create, upon the demand of 10 or more workers, a technological change committee.
This committee would be entitled to receive advance notice of technological change and full information about the impact of proposed technological changes on their jobs, job content and work processes.
The Canadian workplace has been undergoing rapid changes in recent years. This trend will most certainly continue as a result of the Free Trade Agreement. Therefore, it is imperative that Canadian workers are aware of, and receive adequate notice of any technology
June 12, 1989

cal changes that could have an effect on their respective workplaces.
The Free Trade Agreement is certainly not the only reason that Canada is undergoing a structural change in the workplace. Indeed, there are many forces causing businesses in Canada to alter, as they strive toward recapturing markets and improving productivity. The world is in the midst of a technological evolution brought on by innovations in telecommunications and automation. Coupled with the globalization of markets and financial resources, companies must now learn to operate as they would in one huge, open market.
As a result, companies must adapt to the new global realities or they will fall behind others that do adapt. Technological changes in the workplace could thus have a myriad of effects on the Canadian worker, changes which, in many instances, have already occurred. Mainly, the displacement of particular skills by machines; the displacement of some skills by other skills; the development and expansion of some activities and the decline of others, to highlight a few.
Canadian workers are well aware of these developments and realize that they too must make changes. The point of this motion is that they be made aware of any proposed technological changes, as well as the impact of these changes so they can make the necessary adjustments in an adequate amount of time prior to their implementation. It is important to note that in the present Canada Labour Code, an employer must give a union at least 120 days notice of its intention to introduce a technological change into their place of business, a technological change that is likely to: "affect the terms and conditions or security of employment of a significant number of employees".
After a respective union receives such a notice which must include information such as the nature of the technological change, the predicted date of introduction, the estimated number and type of employees likely to be affected, the union may request more detailed information. The union may then apply to the Canada Labour Relations Board for an order that bargaining take place, and until that is completed, the changes may not take place.
The Hon. Member's motion today applies to adequate notification of technological change to a committee of
Technological Change
workers in the workplace. If the workers have direct notification from the employer, they would be in a much better position to evaluate the effects on job retraining and so on so that they can prepare for a smoother and efficient transition. Also, the aforementioned section of the Canada Labour Code does not define what a "significant number of employees" means.
Technological change and the ensuring effect on employment is probably one of the most important concerns of Canadians today. Technological change in the past did not cause significant and persistent high levels of unemployment. Today, technological changes translate into changes in the demand for various occupational skills.
Canadian workers and labour unions are perceived as being against technological change. This perception is based on the notion that workers are worried about their personal welfare by maintaining their jobs and thus security.
I believe workers are well aware of the changes in the global workplace and thus realize that they must change with the times. Not to change would ultimately mean loss of security. What this motion points out is that workers want adequate notice of changes and not last minute notification. Four months notice through their respective unions is not what one would call adequate notice.
In my opinion, workers do not fear the changes in a workplace as much as they are concerned about the uncertainty of these changes. This uncertainty leaves Canadian workers with the feeling of having no influence in a workplace to which they may have dedicated many years of hard work. The older worker, for example, can be left with the feeling that he or she is being dumped for the sake of a more modem way of productivity. We are all well aware that over the past 10 to 15 years there has been a steady decline in labour force participation by older workers, particularly by men in the 50 to 64 age bracket.
When we talk about technological changes in the workplace, a very important variable comes to the forefront. That is education. On average, older workers possess fewer years of formal education than younger workers who are competing in the labour market. Characteristics that older workers possess, such as loyalty, conscientiousness and lower rates of turnover, are often

Technological Change
overlooked for the sake of what a new and technologically trained individual can offer.
Older workers are not against change, they just want adequate notice so as to afford the opportunity to retrain themselves and thus maintain their employment status with their respective employer.
In a study undertaken by the Labour Council of Metropolitan Toronto in 1986, financed by Canada's Technology Impact Research Fund, the council found a lack of corporate planning for the technological change process. The study states:
Only 39 per cent (55 of 140 firms in the sample) report any corporate or strategic plan for the implementation of new technology. Thus, more than 60 per cent of the firms in the sample were ill prepared for the technological innovations that competition supposedly demands.
Other studies concluded that three quarters of employees surveyed were either in favour of technological change, or at least had no opinion against it.
This, I submit, would be because workers came to the realization that a smaller number of relatively secure jobs is better than having to barely survive in an industry that was declining because technological changes were not made.
National studies conducted by the Canadian Paper Workers Union and by the United Steelworkers of America concluded that there was no resistance to technological change. That would seem to be a non issue.
Labour is reasonably open to technological changes that will improve productivity. At the same time, there are some serious concerns about the process of technological change. What is of concern is how technology and the ensuing new work methods are introduced. Inherent in these concerns are three points: First, are the technological changes necessary; second, the minimization of workplace disruption both in terms of displacement of employees and the protection of individual rights and standards; third, the negotiation of compensation for those affected by the displacement of labour.
These are concerns that would be addressed with the establishment of a technological change committee in the workplace. It is important to point out to the House that in a 1985 survey taken by the Ontario Task Force on
Employment and New Technology, it noted that consultation with labour on new technology is the exception rather than the rule. More direct and ongoing consultation is needed between the employer and employee.
I believe that the motion tabled in the House today would be a major step toward legitimizing both parties' interests. Thus, I support the motion. I see it as a major step between both the employer and the employee as we move rapidly toward an increasingly competitive global workplace.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Saskatoon-Dundurn (Mr. Fisher) for having the foresight to bring before the House the important issue of technological change and innovation.
Since taking office in 1984, this Government has made it clear that it had as a priority the promotion and development of technological innovation throughout Canadian society. We strongly believe that Canada's future prosperity largely depends on the country's ability to use technology to its advantage.
We are indeed committed to improve Canada's future international competitiveness through more effective technological application and innovation. We are convinced that workers too will benefit from increasing our competitiveness.
Let me point out that a series of important initiatives have flowed from this priority. It was translated into the creation of a Standing Committee of the House of Commons on Research, Science and Technology, to provide a continuing parliamentary focus on this vital area of national public policy.
As well, it led to the creation of a national advisory board on science and technology to enhance Canada's standing on the world market and a Department of Industry, Science and Technology with a mandate to work toward a closer integration of Canadian industry with Canadian scientific knowledge and technological skills.
In the last five years, this Government has consistently worked at developing a cohesive and coherent technological policy. In fact, the National Council of Science and Technology ministry was especially created to over-
June 12, 1989

see the implementation of a new national science and technology policy.
Many important programs were established to support this policy. Among the most successful is the InnovAction Program which has focused on such critical areas as: technological diffusion, development of strategic technologies, effective use of technologies, human resources for the use of technologies and public education in science and technology.
A particularly successful program is Labour Canada's Technology Impact Program, TIP, which was designed to study how to deal effectively with the adjustment problems arising from the introduction of workplace technologies. This program stems from this Government's awareness that to maximize the gains from any technological applications, there has to be a greater co-operative effort between those implicated in the change when implementing new workplace technologies. Studies such as those carried out by the Economic Council of Canada and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce Task Force on Harnessing Change have clearly supported our view that this partnership is critical to the effective use of new technologies.
Indeed, the Technology Impact Program was specifically created to provide labour organizations with the financial assistance to participate actively in the process of change. Projects carried out under TIP not only focused specifically on the human dimension of change but also involved the full participation of workers and their representatives in the process of change.
More important, all these projects demonstrated how vitally significant labour management co-operation could be to the effective use of technological innovation.
The funds have been used by labour organizations as well as other groups, such as women, disabled workers and older workers to ease their adjustment to the new technology and to explore creative utilizations which might improve the quality of their lives. These projects have ranged right across all sectors of the economy: The construction and auto industries, fishing, forestry, printing, textiles and clothing, health care, education and municipal and provincial Governments, to name just a few.
Technological Change
This Government has addressed the technological change and innovation issue through its series of national and regional conferences on technology and innovation. As recently as a few weeks ago, an important conference on the workplace technology, The Human Dimension, hosted by Labour Canada, attracted a large contingent of business and labour leaders who shared their technological change experiences and discussed ways of making the new technology work for Canada.
This successful event afforded all the participants the opportunity to review how management and labour have, and sometimes have not, succeeded in dealing with the issues that frequently accompany technological change in the workplace. The human dimension of such change was sharply kept in focus throughout the discussions. Among the human impacts of innovation considered were a broad array of human needs such as worker autonomy, meaningful work, ergonomics, health and safety issues, skill requirements and better communication between all those implicated in the change. Together, the participants also looked forward to future developments and to the new, unexplored challenges of implementation strategies which would promote a renewed labour management co-operation. The Canada Labour Code fosters labour management co-operation. The climate of trust that currently characterizes Canadian labour relations must not be undermined.
The Technology Impact Program and the recent conference on the Human dimension of Technological Change have greatly contributed to current knowledge and understanding of effective technological application and innovation in the Canadian workplace.
These initiatives underscore this Government's view that if technology is to be used to improve our well-being, both in the workplace and in Canadian society as a whole, it must be implemented in a humane way with the co-operation of those implicated in the change.

The effects of change are probably felt most keenly in the workplace, since new developments in international trade and the changing nature of the labour force are obliging Canadians to adjust and to seek new ways of carrying out their tasks more successfully. Technological

change also has a considerable impact at work, and that is why I would like to thank Hon. Members for having brought this very important question to the attention of the House.
Madam Speaker, the Speech from the Throne, the labour force development strategy and the Budget reflect this Government's efforts to ensure that Canada will be able to cope with change and will take the necessary steps to do so. Madam Speaker, here is proof that Canada is forging ahead and that change can be made to work to our best advantage.
The five objectives set by the Government for its second mandate are to strengthen the economy, build a caring and compassionate society, protect the environment, foster values that make Canada unique and continue to promote national unity. Madam Speaker, these are the objectives we are resolved to pursue, confident in the resources of this country and with the conviction that any initiative to reduce the deficit can only further these goals.
Madam Speaker, faced with the challenges and opportunities arising from rapidly changing economic and social conditions, both in Canada and abroad, the Canadian Government believes it is even more important to take advantage of the knowledge and skills, expertise and co-operation of all Canadians. Madam Speaker, the Government is firmly resolved to build and support constructive partnerships in which unions, businesses and the Government will come together.
During the last four years. Madam Speaker, we have witnessed a spectacular change in the relationship between unions and employers in the workplace. We have seen a considerable reduction in the frequency of labour disputes and, also very important, we have seen a new and encouraging degree of co-operation away from the bargaining table. Madam Speaker, unions and employers are finding new and often innovative ways of working together to deal with common issues and concerns. There are new, joint initiatives and a co-operative approach to dealing with problems, and all of this is happening across Canada in various sectors of the economy.
The Government supports these efforts by unions and employers, especially at the sectoral level. In this respect, we have seen the development of a number of new and exciting initiatives by industrial unions to deal with the particular concerns of their activity sector.
The most widely known of these initiatives is perhaps the Canadian Steel Trade and Employment Congress, founded in May 1985 by the United Metal Workers of America and major steel producers. Madam Speaker, Labour Canada helped the union and the companies to set up this joint consultation and research body. The Congress has enabled steel workers and producers to deal jointly with the trade and employment issues affecting their sectors. One of their achievements, and in fact the most obvious one, has been the labour force adjustment program, designed specifically for the sector covered by the Congress with the help of a $20 million grant from Employment and Immigration Canada.
The Congress has also been active on the issue of steel imports, so much so that the Government introduced changes in favour of the industry, responding to its needs. In February 1987, the Congress saw the abolition of the general preferential tariff on steel imports from countries such as Korea, Taiwan and Brazil. Madam Speaker, this tariff was unnecessarily favourable to exports from these countries to Canada, despite the fact that they had become very competitive with our own producers. Later that year, a system for monitoring exports, considered by the industry as a way to control steel exports, especially the transshipment of steel to the U.S. market, was implemented.
In the electric and electronic products manufacturing sector, Labour Canada and Employment and Immigration helped a number of businesses and five unions to develop a human resources strategy for their sector. Together, unions and companies in this industry examined training and skills upgrading programs, including a plan for the joint financing of these activities, strategies for implementing technological change and measures to improve the transition between school and work for young graduates.
Such activities will help the electric and electronic products manufacturing industry plan better for, and adjust to the changes arising from increased competition and rapidly evolving technology. The industry will be in a position to train and retrain workers in order to provide
June 12, 1989

them with the skills they will need today and tomorrow. It will be able to introduce new technology effectively, with a minimum of disruption. It will also be able to recruit new young workers and thus provide for the future of the industry. The Unions and the companies will always work together.
Supported by the Government, Madam Speaker, the International Union of Wood workers of America and a number of producers from British Columbia formed the Western Wood Products Forum, in May 1988. This joint research and consultation organization is now looking into important issues such as market access, worker adjustment and the use of forest products. More specifically, the Forum decided that one of its major priorities was establishing a special agreement on plywood. An agreement of this kind would help companies improve a situation that is currently very precarious, and thus make them more competitive on world markets.
In recent months. Labour Canada has engaged in talks and worked to promote new sectoral initiatives with labour and management in a number of industries that are important to the Canadian economy.
The Canadian Steel Trade and Employment Congress, the Western Wood Products Forum and the joint human resources committee of the electrical and electronics manufacturing industry represent a small group of risky businesses, directed jointly by labour and management, that influence unions and employers throughout the country. They represent a trend to greater cooperation and teamwork to solve problems, showing the ability and determination of labour and management to work together, besides at the bargaining table, on questions and concerns of mutual interest.
Madam Speaker, the Government is determined to continue supporting labour and management, to encourage and facilitate dynamic partnerships between unions and employers. In this way, Canadians will be able to meet more effectively the social and economic challenges that we share.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to comment briefly on the motion before the House that the Canada Labour Code be amended to allow all federal jurisdiction workers the right, upon the demand of 10 or more workers, to create a technological change committee. It is envisaged that such technological change committees would be entitled to advance notice of technological change and full information about the impact of proposed technological changes on employment, job content and work processes.
Under the Canadian industrial relations system, adjustment to technological change in the federal jurisdiction is dealt with primarily through the collective bargaining process. To support this process, a number of legislative initiatives have been introduced over the years.
Equally important to the impact of railway run-throughs was the issue of the manner in which technological changes were being introduced by management. Recognizing the important labour-management issue involved, the Government of the day established an independent industrial inquiry commission to explore ways to better manage the introduction of technological change in the context of Canada's economic environment and free collective bargaining system.
The approach eventually adopted by Parliament after hearing from both labour and management involved the placement of requirements in the Canada Labour Code concerning advance notice and the negotiation of the effects of significant changes on employees. The negotiation process component under certain circumstances envisaged eventual access to conciliation procedure, and to strike or lock-out rights under the code.
The Canada Labour Relations Board was designated as the agency responsible for determining questions as to whether notice should have been given in a particular situation and as to whether or not a proposed technological change was of sufficient significance to warrant triggering negotiations during the term of an otherwise closed agreement.
Most important, the parties were encouraged to develop in advance of actual changes their own means of coping with technological change issues through specific

June 12, 1989
Supply
provisions in their collective agreements. If an employer failed to agree to contract provisions and procedures satisfactory to the union, then that employer would be vulnerable to having the collective agreement reopened if significant technological changes were introduced during its term.
These innovative changes introduced into the Canada Labour Code in 1982 had the specific intent of providing a period of notice of the intent to introduce a significant technological change and providing a mechanism for adjudication and redress in cases where notice had not been given. They were also meant to provide a means for reopening an otherwise fixed term and closed collective agreement, in cases where a technological change might adversely affect a significant number of employees. Finally, their intent was to encourage the parties in collective bargaining to adopt their own measures, in advance, to cope with technological changes and to offer exemptions from application of the technological change provisions when such measures were embodied in provisions of a collective agreement.
In essence, the approach, which was eventually adopted by Parliament in 1972, preserved the essentially stabilizing features of the fixed term closed collective agreement. However, it also provided an opportunity to bargain when the basis on which the agreement had been originally negotiated was fundamentally altered by the introduction of new technology.
